questions.prompt: A researcher finds that response time increases approximately linearly with the angular difference between two objects. Which inference is best supported?
questions.explanation: The response-time pattern constrains a mental-rotation account. It is an inference about a process, not direct observation or exact localization.
choices: People may transform an internal representation through intermediate orientations.
The researcher directly observed a thought.
Angular difference changes the number of neurons in the brain.
Behavior alone establishes the exact brain region responsible.
choiceExplanations: A larger angular difference taking longer fits a process that passes through intermediate orientations. Response-time differences provide indirect evidence for a mental transformation.
The researcher measured responses, not thoughts directly. Mental rotation is an explanation inferred from the pattern of behavior.
The manipulation changes the objects' relative orientations. Nothing in these response-time data measures a change in neuron number.
Behavior can constrain a process account, but it cannot by itself locate that process in a particular brain region.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes cognitive psychology from strict behaviorism as presented in this course?
questions.explanation: Cognitive psychology retains objective measurement while explaining behavior in terms of unobserved mental processes.
choices: Cognitive psychology uses only private reports.
Cognitive psychology uses measurable behavior to infer internal processes.
Behaviorism studies only brain scans.
Cognitive psychology rejects experimental evidence.
choiceExplanations: Cognitive psychology does not depend only on private reports. Controlled response times, accuracy, and other observable behavior provide evidence about internal processes.
This preserves objective measurement while allowing hypotheses about representations and operations that cannot be observed directly.
Strict behaviorism emphasizes observable stimulus-response relations. Brain scanning is neither its defining method nor its only subject.
Cognitive accounts must make predictions that experiments can test. Explaining internal processes does not mean rejecting empirical evidence.

questions.prompt: A person can detect individual lines but cannot recognize the object they form. Which interpretation is strongest?
questions.explanation: Recognition can fail despite preserved basic feature detection. The description supports a processing distinction, not an exact diagnosis.
choices: All visual sensation is absent.
The hypothalamus is necessarily damaged.
Association-level processing may be impaired despite some preserved early visual processing.
The optic nerve must be completely severed.
choiceExplanations: Preserved detection of individual lines is evidence that some visual processing remains. A recognition deficit is not equivalent to losing all sensation.
The hypothalamus is associated with homeostatic and endocrine regulation. The vignette does not specifically implicate it or uniquely locate any injury.
Detecting features and recognizing their configuration place different demands on visual processing. Their separation supports a possible higher-level recognition impairment.
Complete loss of the relevant optic-nerve input would not explain preserved visual detection of the lines. The description does not establish optic-nerve damage.

questions.prompt: Which pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: The primary motor and somatosensory regions lie on opposite sides of the central sulcus.
choices: Thalamus: primary endocrine regulation; hypothalamus: all visual edge detection.
Occipital lobe: voluntary motor command; frontal lobe: only hearing.
Hippocampus: myelin formation; amygdala: CSF production.
Precentral cortex: primary motor function; postcentral cortex: primary somatosensory function.
choiceExplanations: The hypothalamus, not the thalamus, is the key endocrine/homeostatic comparison. Visual edge processing involves visual pathways and cortex rather than being assigned to all hypothalamic activity.
Primary motor cortex lies in frontal cortex. Occipital cortex supports vision, and the frontal lobe has many functions beyond hearing.
The hippocampus supports learning and memory rather than producing myelin. The amygdala contributes to emotional processing rather than producing cerebrospinal fluid.
Precentral cortex lies just anterior to the central sulcus and includes primary motor cortex; postcentral cortex lies posterior and includes primary somatosensory cortex.

questions.prompt: A small left primary motor cortex injury causes a right-hand movement deficit. This most directly illustrates:
questions.explanation: Many motor pathways predominantly control the opposite side. This does not imply every brain function is contralateral.
choices: Contralateral organization.
A commissural tract.
A feature-net error.
A sensory neuron receiving hormones.
choiceExplanations: The left cortical site and right-hand deficit are on opposite sides. This is the relevant meaning of contralateral organization in the motor example.
A commissural tract connects hemispheres. The observation instead concerns the relationship between a motor region and the opposite side of the body.
A feature net is a recognition model involving activation among detectors. It does not describe the side relationship in a motor deficit.
The vignette concerns a cortical motor injury and movement, not a sensory neuron's hormonal input. That description does not explain the opposite-side pattern.

questions.prompt: A stimulus becomes stronger after a neuron already reaches firing threshold. Which change best represents greater intensity in a basic rate-code account?
questions.explanation: Action potentials are approximately all-or-none; firing rate and recruitment can carry intensity information.
choices: Each action potential becomes twice as tall.
The neuron can fire more frequently while individual spikes remain similar in amplitude.
Neurotransmitters become electrical wires.
The axon changes from an output structure to an input structure.
choiceExplanations: Once an action potential is generated, its amplitude is approximately stereotyped. Greater stimulus intensity is not normally encoded by making each spike proportionally taller.
In a basic rate code, stronger input can increase the number of spikes per unit time while each spike retains a similar amplitude. Rate changes have physiological limits.
Neurotransmitters remain chemical signals acting at receptors. Stronger input does not convert them into physical electrical wires.
Stimulus intensity does not reverse the neuron's input-output organization. Axons typically conduct output toward terminals.

questions.prompt: The same transmitter can have different effects at different synapses chiefly because:
questions.explanation: Transmitter identity alone is not a sufficient description of the effect; receptors and ion conductances matter.
choices: Every transmitter always excites every neuron.
Postsynaptic neurons have no receptors.
Receptor type and its downstream effects determine the postsynaptic response.
The presynaptic neuron sends a larger action potential to inhibitory cells.
choiceExplanations: Transmitter binding can increase or decrease firing probability. Assuming that every transmitter always excites ignores receptor and conductance differences.
Postsynaptic receptors are precisely what allow a transmitter to affect the receiving cell. Removing them would prevent the proposed receptor-mediated response.
Different receptors and their downstream effects can produce different changes in membrane conductance and firing probability, even for the same transmitter.
Action potentials are not made larger simply because the target is inhibitory. The postsynaptic response depends on receptors and cellular conditions.

questions.prompt: A brain region activates when people view fearful faces. Which claim exceeds the evidence?
questions.explanation: This combines unjustified reverse inference with an unjustified causal claim. Activation alone establishes neither exclusivity nor necessity.
choices: The region's measured signal differs between conditions.
The task and signal are associated.
A control condition is needed to interpret the contrast.
That activation proves fear is the only process occurring and the region is necessary for it.
choiceExplanations: A measured contrast between fearful-face and comparison conditions can support a difference in the recorded signal, assuming the analysis and experiment are sound.
Task-related activation supports an association between the condition and the signal. Association alone makes a more limited claim than causation or exclusivity.
The interpretation depends on what the comparison holds constant. Differences in vision, attention, decisions, or responses could otherwise explain the contrast.
This is the claim that exceeds the evidence: activity does not identify fear as the only possible process, and observing activity does not show that the region is necessary.

questions.prompt: Which method is most appropriate for testing whether disrupting an accessible cortical site changes performance at a specific time?
questions.explanation: TMS perturbs cortical activity; behavior and control stimulation can test a causal contribution and its timing.
choices: TMS with suitable control conditions.
A structural MRI alone.
A questionnaire about head size.
Uncontrolled comparison of two activation maps.
choiceExplanations: TMS can perturb an accessible cortical site at selected times. Comparing behavior with sham, control-site, or control-time conditions tests a causal contribution.
Structural MRI shows anatomy. A structural image alone neither disrupts the site nor tests whether disruption changes performance at a particular moment.
A head-size questionnaire supplies neither a localized neural intervention nor precise timing of a processing stage.
Uncontrolled activation maps provide observational contrasts. They do not isolate the effects of disrupting a site and cannot exclude basic confounds.

questions.prompt: Among noninvasive methods discussed in 105, which comparison is generally correct?
questions.explanation: Electrical recording and structural/hemodynamic imaging measure different signals and have different strengths.
choices: EEG gives better anatomical localization than structural MRI.
EEG offers high temporal resolution; MRI/fMRI offer finer spatial localization.
fMRI measures individual action potentials with millisecond resolution.
All methods directly measure the same neuronal event.
choiceExplanations: EEG measures electrical population activity at the scalp and faces a difficult source-localization problem. Structural MRI generally gives finer anatomical detail.
EEG can track millisecond-scale changes, whereas MRI provides detailed anatomy and fMRI generally localizes task-related changes more finely in space. Their strengths differ.
fMRI measures a delayed hemodynamic signal, not individual action potentials. Fast image sampling does not turn that signal into millisecond spike recording.
These methods measure different things: electrical activity, tissue structure, or blood-related changes. Their signals and limitations are not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly follows the main retinal signal toward cortex?
questions.explanation: Photoreceptors transduce light; bipolar cells relay within the retina; ganglion axons form the optic nerve. LGN is the main thalamic relay before V1.
choices: Ganglion -> rod/cone -> bipolar -> LGN -> V1.
Rod/cone -> ganglion -> bipolar -> V1 -> LGN.
Rod/cone -> bipolar -> ganglion -> optic nerve -> LGN -> V1.
LGN -> optic nerve -> rod/cone -> V1.
choiceExplanations: Photoreceptors transduce light before bipolar and ganglion-cell stages. This order incorrectly places ganglion cells before the photoreceptors.
Bipolar cells relay before ganglion cells in the main retinal sequence. The LGN also precedes V1 in the main retino-geniculo-cortical pathway.
Rods and cones transduce light, bipolar cells relay within the retina, and ganglion-cell axons form the optic nerve. The main thalamic relay is LGN before V1.
This reverses the input sequence. Light is transduced in retinal photoreceptors, and retinal signals travel toward LGN and cortex rather than starting in LGN.

questions.prompt: An ON-center/OFF-surround ganglion cell is tested with equal-intensity stimuli. Which should produce its strongest response under the simple center-surround model?
questions.explanation: Center illumination excites and surround illumination opposes that excitation. Uniform illumination produces partial cancellation.
choices: Light only in its surround.
Uniform light over its center and entire surround.
No light anywhere necessarily causes its maximum response.
Light confined to its center with a dark surround.
choiceExplanations: Illuminating only the OFF surround opposes the ON-center cell's response. It would tend to suppress firing relative to its baseline rather than maximize excitation.
Center excitation and surround inhibition partly cancel under uniform illumination. The response is typically smaller than with isolated center illumination.
An ON-center cell is excited by light in its center. Darkness everywhere does not provide that center-surround contrast and need not maximize firing.
This stimulates the excitatory center without illuminating the antagonistic surround. It therefore predicts the strongest response among these choices in the simple model.

questions.prompt: A V1 neuron fires most for a bar tilted 45 degrees and less for nearby orientations. This demonstrates:
questions.explanation: A tuning curve relates firing rate to a stimulus dimension, here orientation, within the neuron's receptive field.
choices: Orientation tuning.
That the neuron responds only to whole faces.
That its receptive field is the entire retina.
That it has no spontaneous activity.
choiceExplanations: Firing varies with the bar's orientation and peaks near a preferred angle. That relationship is orientation tuning.
The stimuli are oriented bars, not whole faces. A response preference for a bar orientation does not establish face selectivity.
Orientation tuning describes which feature values change firing. It does not establish the spatial extent of the receptive field, much less the entire retina.
The tuning result compares responses to stimuli. Without a baseline measurement, it says nothing about whether the neuron fires spontaneously.

questions.prompt: A patient can describe an object's identity but struggles to use vision to guide a reach toward it. Which distinction is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Identity and visually guided action can be differentially affected. Real behavior involves interacting pathways.
choices: Sympathetic versus parasympathetic division.
Ventral identity processing versus dorsal spatial/action processing.
Rods versus microglia.
Early selection versus attenuation.
choiceExplanations: Sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions concern autonomic regulation. They are not the main distinction between identifying an object and guiding a reach visually.
Ventral-stream processing emphasizes identity, while dorsal-stream processing emphasizes space and visually guided action. Differential impairment is consistent with those broad contributions.
Rods are photoreceptors and microglia are immune-related glia. This contrast does not explain preserved identity judgments with impaired visually guided action.
Early selection and attenuation concern attentional selection of input. They do not directly name the visual identity-versus-action distinction tested here.

questions.prompt: In a familiar sentence, an ambiguous character is read as a letter; in a number sequence, it is read as a digit. This best illustrates:
questions.explanation: Context changes interpretation; stimulus features still constrain which interpretations are plausible.
choices: Only retinal sensitivity.
Contralateral motor control.
Top-down influence on interpretation of the same input.
The absence of bottom-up processing.
choiceExplanations: The same visual input receives different interpretations depending on context. Retinal sensitivity alone cannot explain why a word versus number sequence changes the interpretation.
Contralateral motor control concerns opposite-side movement organization. The example concerns perception of an ambiguous character rather than a motor pathway.
Knowledge of the surrounding word or number sequence biases interpretation. That is a top-down influence acting on the same sensory shape.
Bottom-up features are still present and constrain possible readings. A contextual influence does not imply that sensory evidence has stopped contributing.

questions.prompt: Which depth cue requires comparing the two eyes' images?
questions.explanation: Perspective, occlusion, and texture gradients can be available to a single eye.
choices: Linear perspective.
Interposition.
Texture gradient.
Binocular disparity.
choiceExplanations: Linear perspective uses the projected convergence of lines with distance. That pattern can be seen in a single eye's image.
Interposition uses one object's occlusion of another. A single eye can register the occlusion, so eye-to-eye comparison is unnecessary.
Texture gradient uses changes in the size or density of projected texture. These changes can be available to one eye.
The two eyes view a scene from slightly different positions. Comparing those image differences provides binocular disparity, which requires both views.

questions.prompt: In a feature net, a partly obscured letter is identified more readily in a familiar word. Which explanation fits?
questions.explanation: Activation can accumulate across levels. Context can help resolve ambiguity but can also bias recognition toward an incorrect familiar interpretation.
choices: Partial evidence and context can jointly raise a candidate detector above threshold.
The retina receives more photons because the word is familiar.
Feature detectors cannot make errors.
Only an exact stored photograph can support recognition.
choiceExplanations: Residual feature evidence can combine with contextual support to activate a letter candidate sufficiently for recognition. Perfect visibility is not required in this account.
Familiarity does not cause the displayed word to deliver more photons to the retina. The proposed benefit is in processing and interpretation of the available input.
Thresholded, evidence-weighted recognition can select a plausible but wrong candidate. Feature nets can explain errors as well as successful recognition.
A feature net uses combinations of features and candidate activation rather than requiring a perfect stored photograph to match every view.

questions.prompt: Recognition by Components primarily proposes that objects are recognized from:
questions.explanation: Geons and their arrangement support recognition across many views when diagnostic structure remains visible.
choices: A unique neuron for every exact retinal picture.
Basic volumetric components and their spatial relations.
Only the object's color.
Only the observer's current viewpoint.
choiceExplanations: RBC does not require a unique unit for every exact retinal image. It proposes reusable volumetric components and relations that can support recognition across views.
RBC emphasizes geons and how those components are arranged. Both component identity and spatial relations help distinguish objects.
Color can be useful in recognition, but color alone is not RBC's defining structural account. Different objects can share the same color.
RBC predicts useful robustness across views that preserve diagnostic structure. It does not reduce recognition to the observer's current viewpoint alone.

questions.prompt: Which finding is most consistent with an important role for configural processing in face recognition?
questions.explanation: Inversion disrupts the usual use of relations among facial parts; this does not imply that individual features play no role.
choices: Faces are always recognized perfectly.
Inverting a face never changes recognition.
Inversion disproportionately disrupts face recognition relative to many ordinary objects.
Recognizing a face uses no features.
choiceExplanations: Perfect recognition is not a prediction required by configural processing. Faces can be misidentified, and this claim supplies no evidence about relations among parts.
A lack of inversion effects would not provide the proposed evidence that normal face processing relies strongly on its usual configuration.
A disproportionate inversion cost is consistent with disruption of the usual use of facial-part relationships. It supports configural contributions without proving an exclusive face-only mechanism.
Configural processing concerns relationships among features; it does not eliminate the features themselves. Both parts and their arrangement can contribute.

questions.prompt: A strict early-selection model predicts that unattended input is normally filtered primarily:
questions.explanation: Physical-channel selection precedes full meaning analysis in the strict version; unattended semantic effects challenge it.
choices: After complete semantic interpretation of every item.
Only after a spoken response.
Only after long-term memory retrieval.
On the basis of physical characteristics before full semantic processing.
choiceExplanations: Filtering after complete meaning analysis is the late-selection alternative. Strict early selection places filtering before full semantic processing.
A spoken response occurs after substantial processing and response preparation. It is not the early, physical-channel filter proposed by this model.
Long-term retrieval is not the defining selection boundary. The strict account selects by physical properties before full semantic analysis of unattended input.
The strict early account uses physical/channel characteristics to select input before full meaning analysis. Unattended semantic effects are important challenges to this version.

questions.prompt: An attenuation model handles occasional detection of one's name in an unattended channel by proposing that:
questions.explanation: Reduced signal strength plus unequal detection thresholds permits occasional breakthrough without claiming all unattended content is fully processed.
choices: Unattended signals are weakened, while especially low-threshold items can still be recognized.
The unattended channel is always completely erased.
Every unattended word receives full conscious attention.
The auditory nerve reverses direction.
choiceExplanations: Attenuation weakens unattended input rather than deleting it. An especially low-threshold item, such as one's name, can occasionally reach recognition despite the weakened signal.
Complete erasure would leave no unattended name signal to exceed a threshold. That makes occasional breakthrough difficult for a strict all-or-none filter.
Occasional detection of a salient item does not establish full conscious attention to every unattended word. Unequal thresholds allow selective breakthrough.
The auditory nerve does not need to reverse its direction for name detection. The explanation concerns signal strength and recognition thresholds.

questions.prompt: A highly predictive cue speeds valid trials but slows invalid trials relative to neutral trials. This pattern most strongly suggests:
questions.explanation: Preparing expected detectors yields benefits and can leave unexpected targets disadvantaged.
choices: Only cost-free stimulus-driven priming.
Expectation-based allocation of limited resources.
A larger action potential on valid trials.
That expectations cannot affect perception.
choiceExplanations: A purely cost-free facilitation account can explain valid-trial benefits but not the added disadvantage on invalid trials relative to neutral.
Preparing for a likely target improves expected processing while leaving unexpected input disadvantaged. Both valid benefits and invalid costs fit limited-resource expectation-based allocation.
The result concerns behavioral response time. It neither measures spike amplitude nor requires larger action potentials to explain the benefit.
Performance changes systematically with predictive cues. That pattern is evidence that expectations can affect processing, subject to appropriate controls.

questions.prompt: A single red item among blue items is found with little set-size cost; a red X among red Os and blue Xs takes longer as items increase. Which explanation fits classic FIT?
questions.explanation: The contrast is the classic feature/conjunction pattern, although search behavior can be modified by task and display conditions.
choices: Both searches require no attention.
The second search tests only retinal brightness.
Separate feature maps support feature search; conjunctions require binding features at locations with attention.
The first search necessarily involves identifying every item serially.
choiceExplanations: Classic FIT assigns an important role to attention in binding conjunctions at locations. The growing conjunction-search cost is inconsistent with assuming neither search needs attention.
The target is defined by a combination of color and shape, not brightness alone. The distractors share each individual target feature.
A unique feature can stand out in a feature map. A conjunction requires assigning features to the same item/location, accounting for the classic greater set-size cost.
A small feature-search slope does not require serial identification of every distractor. Efficient feature search is the contrast with the more demanding conjunction search.

questions.prompt: After a very brief display, a person reports a red X when the display contained a red O and a blue X. The report is an example of:
questions.explanation: Features were detected but incorrectly combined, consistent with a role for attention in feature binding.
choices: A motor action potential.
Perceptual size constancy.
An association tract.
An illusory conjunction.
choiceExplanations: An action potential is a neural electrical event. It does not name the perceptual error of combining the color of one item with the shape of another.
Size constancy concerns perceived object size despite changes in retinal size or distance. No such size-distance change is described here.
An association tract is a same-hemisphere cortical connection. It does not name the mistaken assignment of detected visual features.
Red and X were present, but on different objects. Reporting a red X incorrectly binds available features, making this an illusory conjunction.

questions.prompt: Which prediction best combines task-specific pools with a task-general bottleneck?
questions.explanation: Reduced modality overlap does not remove shared executive-control or response-selection demands.
choices: Two tasks in different modalities can still interfere when both require response selection.
Different modalities guarantee no interference.
Practice increases resource demand on every task.
Two equally difficult verbal tasks never compete.
choiceExplanations: Different sensory modalities can reduce competition for modality-specific resources, yet both tasks may still need a shared response-selection or executive stage.
Separate modalities do not guarantee separate control and response resources. A task-general bottleneck can still cause cross-modal interference.
Practice can reduce attention demands or improve coordination; it does not inherently increase every task's resource demand.
Two demanding verbal tasks are likely to overlap in task-specific resources. The claim that they never compete contradicts the task-specific-pool account.

questions.prompt: Define a mental process. Give two examples. Explain why a list of active brain regions alone does not specify the process being used.
questions.explanation: A mental process transforms, selects, stores, retrieves, or uses information. Examples include interpreting a word and directing attention. Regional activation identifies a physical correlate without uniquely specifying the computation. Behavioral tasks and competing predictions are needed to distinguish explanations; brain and behavioral evidence complement one another.
rubric: A mental process transforms, selects, stores, retrieves, or uses information.
Examples include interpreting a word and directing attention.
Regional activation identifies a physical correlate without uniquely specifying the computation.
Behavioral tasks and competing predictions are needed to distinguish explanations; brain and behavioral evidence complement one another.
commonMistakes: Naming a region is not the same as specifying an operation. A location may participate in several computations; explain what information changes and how the task tests that proposed process.

questions.prompt: Compare introspection, strict behaviorism, and cognitive psychology by their evidence and assumptions. Give one limitation of introspection.
questions.explanation: Introspection uses reports of conscious experience to investigate mental life. Strict behaviorism prioritizes observable stimulus-response relations while setting aside internal mental explanations. Cognitive psychology uses objective behavior to infer internal representations/processes. Private reports are difficult to verify independently and do not reveal all unconscious processing.
rubric: Introspection uses reports of conscious experience to investigate mental life.
Strict behaviorism prioritizes observable stimulus-response relations while setting aside internal mental explanations.
Cognitive psychology uses objective behavior to infer internal representations/processes.
Private reports are difficult to verify independently and do not reveal all unconscious processing.
commonMistakes: Do not equate cognitive psychology with introspection or claim that behaviorists measured nothing. Cognitive psychology also measures behavior, but uses it to test internal-process explanations; private reports alone are not independently verifiable.

questions.prompt: In a hypothetical experiment, correct responses at 0, 60, and 120 degrees take 500, 650, and 800 ms. Identify the manipulation and measure. Explain how inferring mental rotation illustrates the transcendental method, and why this is not proof of a unique mechanism.
questions.explanation: Angular disparity is manipulated; correct-response latency is measured. Latency increases by 150 ms per 60 degrees, or 2.5 ms/degree. The transcendental method works backward from observable effects to infer hidden processes capable of producing them. The response-time pattern supports an internal transformation such as mental rotation. Alternative mechanisms and confounds must be compared. Inferring a process from its consequences is not direct observation or proof that it is the only possible explanation.
rubric: Angular disparity is manipulated; correct-response latency is measured.
Latency increases by 150 ms per 60 degrees, or 2.5 ms/degree.

The transcendental method works backward from observable effects to infer hidden processes capable of producing them. The response-time pattern supports an internal transformation such as mental rotation.
Alternative mechanisms and confounds must be compared. Inferring a process from its consequences is not direct observation or proof that it is the only possible explanation.
commonMistakes: Angular disparity is the manipulated variable, not response time. The slope is 300 ms divided by 120 degrees, not 800 divided by 120; an intercept includes processing that occurs even at zero disparity.

questions.prompt: Distinguish cognitive psychology, neuroscience, cognitive neuroscience, and AI/computational modeling using one question each could ask about recognizing a face.
questions.explanation: Cognitive psychology asks what representations or operations explain recognition behavior. Neuroscience asks how neurons/circuits operate. Cognitive neuroscience relates recognition processes to neural systems. AI/modeling implements candidate recognition procedures and compares outputs with behavior; matching accuracy alone does not prove human mechanism equivalence.
rubric: Cognitive psychology asks what representations or operations explain recognition behavior.
Neuroscience asks how neurons/circuits operate.
Cognitive neuroscience relates recognition processes to neural systems.
AI/modeling implements candidate recognition procedures and compares outputs with behavior; matching accuracy alone does not prove human mechanism equivalence.
commonMistakes: Matching a computer model's accuracy to a person's does not establish identical mechanisms. Different procedures can produce the same output, so compare process-sensitive predictions as well as overall success.

questions.prompt: Design a behavioral experiment that could distinguish two explanations of attention. Specify a manipulation, a measure, differing predictions, and a control.
questions.explanation: Manipulate target-cue validity while holding target visibility constant. Measure response time and accuracy. An expectation account predicts valid benefits and invalid costs, whereas a strictly cost-free facilitation account lacks invalid costs. Include a neutral-cue baseline and comparable sensory/motor demands. Other coherent designs earn credit.
rubric: Manipulate target-cue validity while holding target visibility constant.
Measure response time and accuracy.
An expectation account predicts valid benefits and invalid costs, whereas a strictly cost-free facilitation account lacks invalid costs.
Include a neutral-cue baseline and comparable sensory/motor demands. Other coherent designs earn credit.
commonMistakes: A study in which both explanations predict the same result does not distinguish them. Without neutral cues, a valid-invalid gap also cannot separate facilitation from a cost to unexpected targets.

questions.prompt: Identify regions 1-4 on the schematic and give one broad function for each. State front/back before identifying them.
questions.explanation: Region 1 is frontal: voluntary movement, planning, attention, or inhibition. Region 2 is parietal: somatosensation or spatial processing. Region 3 is temporal: hearing, aspects of recognition/language, or memory systems. Region 4 is occipital: visual processing. Front is at left, back at right in this schematic; functions are broad, not exclusive.
rubric: Region 1 is frontal: voluntary movement, planning, attention, or inhibition.
Region 2 is parietal: somatosensation or spatial processing.
Region 3 is temporal: hearing, aspects of recognition/language, or memory systems.
Region 4 is occipital: visual processing. Front is at left, back at right in this schematic; functions are broad, not exclusive.
commonMistakes: Do not identify a lobe by its drawing color or treat one broad function as its exclusive job. First orient front and back, then use the central/lateral sulci and relative positions to locate the lobes.

questions.prompt: Using the lateral brain schematic, name landmarks 5 and 6. Locate primary motor and somatosensory cortex relative to landmark 5. Explain why location matters more than diagram color.
questions.explanation: Landmark 5 marks the central sulcus. Landmark 6 marks the lateral sulcus/fissure. Primary motor cortex is anterior to the central sulcus; primary somatosensory cortex is posterior. Color is an illustration convention; spatial landmarks and anatomical relationships determine identity.
rubric: Landmark 5 marks the central sulcus.
Landmark 6 marks the lateral sulcus/fissure.
Primary motor cortex is anterior to the central sulcus; primary somatosensory cortex is posterior.
Color is an illustration convention; spatial landmarks and anatomical relationships determine identity.
commonMistakes: Swapping precentral and postcentral cortex reverses the motor-sensory relationship. The central sulcus separates frontal from parietal cortex; the lateral sulcus is a different landmark associated with the temporal boundary.

questions.prompt: Describe the CNS/PNS hierarchy. Add sensory/afferent and motor/efferent directions. Distinguish somatic and autonomic function.
questions.explanation: CNS includes brain and spinal cord; PNS includes neural structures outside them. Afferent pathways carry sensory information toward CNS; efferent pathways carry output away. Somatic pathways serve bodily sensation and skeletal muscle control. Autonomic pathways regulate organs/glands; sympathetic arousal and parasympathetic recovery are useful broad subdivisions.
rubric: CNS includes brain and spinal cord; PNS includes neural structures outside them.
Afferent pathways carry sensory information toward CNS; efferent pathways carry output away.
Somatic pathways serve bodily sensation and skeletal muscle control.
Autonomic pathways regulate organs/glands; sympathetic arousal and parasympathetic recovery are useful broad subdivisions.
commonMistakes: Afferent and efferent are directions relative to a reference, not synonyms for excitatory and inhibitory. Here, sensory input travels toward CNS and motor output away; autonomic activity is not limited to conscious skeletal movement.

questions.prompt: Using the four structures emphasized in 105's introductory limbic/subcortical discussion, distinguish thalamus, hypothalamus, amygdala, and hippocampus by broad location and function.
questions.explanation: Thalamus is deep and near the midline; it relays much sensory information to cortex, with smell the initial-relay exception. Hypothalamus lies below thalamus and regulates bodily needs/homeostasis and neural/endocrine control. Amygdala lies in anterior medial temporal regions and contributes to threat and other emotional processing, not fear alone. Hippocampus lies in medial temporal regions, posterior to amygdala, and supports new learning/memory formation. The introductory grouping is a course convention; limbic-system boundaries vary.
rubric: Thalamus is deep and near the midline; it relays much sensory information to cortex, with smell the initial-relay exception.
Hypothalamus lies below thalamus and regulates bodily needs/homeostasis and neural/endocrine control.
Amygdala lies in anterior medial temporal regions and contributes to threat and other emotional processing, not fear alone.
Hippocampus lies in medial temporal regions, posterior to amygdala, and supports new learning/memory formation. The introductory grouping is a course convention; limbic-system boundaries vary.
commonMistakes: The thalamus and hypothalamus are not interchangeable: sensory relaying differs from endocrine/homeostatic regulation. Likewise, calling the hippocampus all memory or the amygdala only fear overstates their roles within larger systems.

questions.prompt: Distinguish a primary projection area from an association area. Locate primary motor, somatosensory, visual, and auditory cortex by lobe or landmark. Explain why the hand occupies a disproportionate part of a cortical body map.
questions.explanation: Primary projection areas have organized sensory or motor maps closely related to input/output, such as body, visual-field, or sound-property maps. Primary motor cortex is in frontal cortex just anterior to the central sulcus; primary somatosensory cortex is in parietal cortex just posterior to it. Primary visual cortex is in the occipital lobe; primary auditory cortex is in the temporal lobe. Association cortex integrates/interprets information and supports complex cognition. Cortical territory reflects sensory sensitivity or motor precision, not simply body-part size. A large hand representation does not mean the hand is the largest body part.
rubric: Primary projection areas have organized sensory or motor maps closely related to input/output, such as body, visual-field, or sound-property maps.
Primary motor cortex is in frontal cortex just anterior to the central sulcus; primary somatosensory cortex is in parietal cortex just posterior to it.
Primary visual cortex is in the occipital lobe; primary auditory cortex is in the temporal lobe. Association cortex integrates/interprets information and supports complex cognition.
Cortical territory reflects sensory sensitivity or motor precision, not simply body-part size. A large hand representation does not mean the hand is the largest body part.
commonMistakes: The cortical body map is not a scale drawing of body size. Disproportionate hand territory reflects fine motor control or sensory processing demands; primary sensory/motor areas also differ from association cortex.

questions.prompt: Distinguish apraxia, agnosia, aphasia, and hemispatial neglect using a concrete example for each.
questions.explanation: Apraxia: difficulty performing learned purposeful actions not explained by simple weakness, such as pantomiming tool use. Agnosia: impaired recognition despite sufficient basic sensation, such as failing to identify a seen object. Aphasia: impaired language, such as difficulty producing or understanding speech. Neglect: failing to attend/respond to contralesional space, such as omitting the left half of a drawing.
rubric: Apraxia: difficulty performing learned purposeful actions not explained by simple weakness, such as pantomiming tool use.
Agnosia: impaired recognition despite sufficient basic sensation, such as failing to identify a seen object.
Aphasia: impaired language, such as difficulty producing or understanding speech.
Neglect: failing to attend/respond to contralesional space, such as omitting the left half of a drawing.
commonMistakes: A symptom label must describe the impaired operation, not just any poor performance. Weakness alone is not apraxia, basic blindness alone is not agnosia, and neglect is an attentional deficit rather than automatically a sensory field loss.

questions.prompt: A patient can see isolated items on both sides when prompted but spontaneously eats only food on the right side of a plate. Explain the relevant syndrome, likely side of brain injury in the common pattern, and why this differs from blindness.
questions.explanation: The behavior suggests left hemispatial neglect. A common pattern follows right hemisphere/parietal attention-network injury. The deficit concerns attention/representation of space, not necessarily loss of basic visual input. Preserved detection when cued helps distinguish it from a primary visual field loss; clinical testing is needed and both conditions can coexist.
rubric: The behavior suggests left hemispatial neglect.
A common pattern follows right hemisphere/parietal attention-network injury.
The deficit concerns attention/representation of space, not necessarily loss of basic visual input.
Preserved detection when cued helps distinguish it from a primary visual field loss; clinical testing is needed and both conditions can coexist.
commonMistakes: Failing to report left-side items is not enough to diagnose blindness. Preserved detection with prompting supports an attentional account; right-hemisphere injury is common for left neglect, but the vignette cannot uniquely locate a lesion.

questions.prompt: A patient continues sorting cards by color after the rule changes to number. Explain the error, the relevant broad cortical system, and why the problem is not simply failure to see numbers.
questions.explanation: This is perseveration: persistence of a previously relevant response/rule. It suggests executive-control/prefrontal dysfunction. Switching goals and inhibiting the old rule are impaired. Verify preserved number discrimination and rule comprehension before attributing errors to executive control.
rubric: This is perseveration: persistence of a previously relevant response/rule.
It suggests executive-control/prefrontal dysfunction.
Switching goals and inhibiting the old rule are impaired.
Verify preserved number discrimination and rule comprehension before attributing errors to executive control.
commonMistakes: Continuing the old rule is perseveration, not automatically inability to perceive the new sorting feature. Check whether numbers are visible and the new rule understood before concluding that executive switching is impaired.

questions.prompt: Define dorsal/ventral, anterior/posterior, medial/lateral, and contralateral/ipsilateral for a forebrain diagram. Give one correct relationship.
questions.explanation: Dorsal/superior is toward the top and ventral/inferior toward the bottom of the forebrain. Anterior/rostral is front; posterior/caudal is back. Medial is toward the midline; lateral is away. Contralateral is opposite side; ipsilateral is same side. Example: hypothalamus is ventral to thalamus. Direction conventions change along the bent neuraxis; this prompt specifies forebrain.
rubric: Dorsal/superior is toward the top and ventral/inferior toward the bottom of the forebrain.
Anterior/rostral is front; posterior/caudal is back.
Medial is toward the midline; lateral is away.
Contralateral is opposite side; ipsilateral is same side. Example: hypothalamus is ventral to thalamus. Direction conventions change along the bent neuraxis; this prompt specifies forebrain.
commonMistakes: Left/right and medial/lateral are not equivalent: either hemisphere has medial and lateral locations. Also do not apply a forebrain top-bottom convention unchanged to every part of the bent neuraxis.

questions.prompt: Describe a typical neuron, including dendrites, soma, axon hillock, axon, myelin, and terminals. Trace typical information flow and distinguish input, integration, and output.
questions.explanation: Dendrites and soma commonly receive synaptic inputs. Integration near the hillock/initial segment determines whether threshold is reached. Action potentials propagate along the axon; myelin promotes efficient rapid conduction. Terminals release transmitter onto the next cell. A correct description must preserve this input-integration-output organization.
rubric: Dendrites and soma commonly receive synaptic inputs.
Integration near the hillock/initial segment determines whether threshold is reached.
Action potentials propagate along the axon; myelin promotes efficient rapid conduction.
Terminals release transmitter onto the next cell. A correct description must preserve this input-integration-output organization.
commonMistakes: Do not reverse dendrites and axon terminals or describe myelin as the chemical messenger. Inputs are integrated before an action potential propagates toward terminals; transmitter release is the typical output to another cell.

questions.prompt: Describe neural communication from an incoming postsynaptic potential in neuron A through a postsynaptic effect in neuron B. Separate electrical and chemical events.
questions.explanation: Graded inputs in A combine and may reach threshold at the trigger region. An electrical action potential propagates along A's axon. Terminal depolarization triggers transmitter release from vesicles into the synaptic cleft. Transmitter binds B's receptors and changes ion-channel activity/postsynaptic potential. Calcium coupling and clearance add useful detail but are not separate required points here.
rubric: Graded inputs in A combine and may reach threshold at the trigger region.
An electrical action potential propagates along A's axon.
Terminal depolarization triggers transmitter release from vesicles into the synaptic cleft.
Transmitter binds B's receptors and changes ion-channel activity/postsynaptic potential. Calcium coupling and clearance add useful detail but are not separate required points here.
commonMistakes: An action potential does not physically leap across a typical chemical synaptic cleft. Electrical propagation triggers chemical release, and receptor binding in the next cell produces a new electrical influence that may or may not reach threshold.

questions.prompt: Compare a postsynaptic potential and an action potential in amplitude, location, summation, and propagation.
questions.explanation: Postsynaptic potentials are graded and commonly arise in dendrites/soma; APs are approximately all-or-none and begin near the initial segment. Postsynaptic potentials can sum spatially/temporally. APs regenerate along axons rather than fading like passive graded potentials. Increasing input usually changes firing probability/rate rather than AP height.
rubric: Postsynaptic potentials are graded and commonly arise in dendrites/soma; APs are approximately all-or-none and begin near the initial segment.
Postsynaptic potentials can sum spatially/temporally.
APs regenerate along axons rather than fading like passive graded potentials.
Increasing input usually changes firing probability/rate rather than AP height.
commonMistakes: Summation applies to graded postsynaptic potentials, not to adding the heights of ordinary action potentials. Stronger input usually affects spike probability or rate, while regenerating spikes do not simply fade along the axon.

questions.prompt: Explain excitation and inhibition in terms of firing probability. Explain how a cell can receive both without necessarily firing and why transmitter name alone is insufficient.
questions.explanation: Excitation increases the likelihood of reaching firing threshold. Inhibition reduces that likelihood through its effects on membrane conductance/potential. Combined inputs determine the net effect; excitation does not guarantee an AP. Receptor type, ion channels, and ionic conditions determine the effect of transmitter binding.
rubric: Excitation increases the likelihood of reaching firing threshold.
Inhibition reduces that likelihood through its effects on membrane conductance/potential.
Combined inputs determine the net effect; excitation does not guarantee an AP.
Receptor type, ion channels, and ionic conditions determine the effect of transmitter binding.
commonMistakes: One excitatory input does not guarantee a spike, and a transmitter name alone does not fix the response. Competing inputs and receptor-dependent conductances determine whether the receiving cell reaches threshold.

questions.prompt: Correct this explanation: 'An electrical impulse jumps across the empty synapse into the next cell; stronger stimuli make taller impulses; every transmitter enters the next cell to excite it.'
questions.explanation: In a typical chemical synapse, transmitter diffuses across the cleft rather than an AP physically jumping it. Transmitter binds receptors; it need not enter the cell interior. Stimulus strength can be encoded by firing frequency/recruitment, not taller APs. Postsynaptic effects can be excitatory or inhibitory, depending on receptors/conductances.
rubric: In a typical chemical synapse, transmitter diffuses across the cleft rather than an AP physically jumping it.
Transmitter binds receptors; it need not enter the cell interior.
Stimulus strength can be encoded by firing frequency/recruitment, not taller APs.
Postsynaptic effects can be excitatory or inhibitory, depending on receptors/conductances.
commonMistakes: Repair all three errors rather than only one: chemical transmission uses receptor binding across the cleft, stronger stimuli need not make taller spikes, and postsynaptic effects can decrease as well as increase firing probability.

questions.prompt: Compare CT, structural MRI, PET, fMRI, EEG/ERP, single-unit recording, and TMS. For each state its signal/intervention, useful role or resolution, and a limitation. Identify which can provide controlled experimental causal evidence.
questions.explanation: CT uses X-rays to show anatomy. It helps detect structural abnormalities but uses ionizing radiation and does not directly measure task-related neural timing. Structural MRI uses tissue-dependent magnetic-resonance contrast to show detailed anatomy. It is noninvasive and spatially precise but does not directly record moment-to-moment neural firing. PET uses an injected radioactive tracer to measure aspects of physiology. It can map metabolism or receptor-related processes, but requires a tracer and has relatively slow temporal resolution. fMRI measures BOLD changes. It provides fine functional spatial localization but is an indirect, slow hemodynamic measure; activation alone indicates involvement rather than necessity. EEG measures scalp electrical population activity; ERPs are event-locked averages. Their millisecond timing is strong, but source localization is limited. Single-unit recording samples spikes from individual neurons with excellent spatial and temporal specificity. It is invasive and samples limited cells/regions. TMS induces cortical electrical currents to perturb activity. Controlled changes in performance can test causal contribution, but conventional targeting is mainly superficial and needs sham/site/time and nonspecific-effect controls.
rubric: CT uses X-rays to show anatomy. It helps detect structural abnormalities but uses ionizing radiation and does not directly measure task-related neural timing.
Structural MRI uses tissue-dependent magnetic-resonance contrast to show detailed anatomy. It is noninvasive and spatially precise but does not directly record moment-to-moment neural firing.
PET uses an injected radioactive tracer to measure aspects of physiology. It can map metabolism or receptor-related processes, but requires a tracer and has relatively slow temporal resolution.
fMRI measures BOLD changes. It provides fine functional spatial localization but is an indirect, slow hemodynamic measure; activation alone indicates involvement rather than necessity.
EEG measures scalp electrical population activity; ERPs are event-locked averages. Their millisecond timing is strong, but source localization is limited.
Single-unit recording samples spikes from individual neurons with excellent spatial and temporal specificity. It is invasive and samples limited cells/regions.

TMS induces cortical electrical currents to perturb activity. Controlled changes in performance can test causal contribution, but conventional targeting is mainly superficial and needs sham/site/time and nonspecific-effect controls.
commonMistakes: Do not merge structural MRI with functional BOLD or call EEG a blood-flow measure. Also separate observation from intervention: recording task-related activity alone does not establish necessity, whereas controlled TMS can test causal contribution.

questions.prompt: Explain reverse inference using this claim: 'Region R is often active during emotion. R is active now, therefore the person is experiencing fear.' Distinguish this problem from the necessity question.
questions.explanation: The argument infers a mental state from activity in a region associated with that state. R may support many processes, and emotion is broader than fear. Selectivity/base rates and alternatives are needed to assess the inference. Necessity is a separate causal claim: observing activity does not show that disrupting R would impair the task.
rubric: The argument infers a mental state from activity in a region associated with that state.
R may support many processes, and emotion is broader than fear.
Selectivity/base rates and alternatives are needed to assess the inference.
Necessity is a separate causal claim: observing activity does not show that disrupting R would impair the task.
commonMistakes: If fear can activate R, it does not follow that every activation of R means fear. Even a highly selective association would leave the separate causal question of whether the function depends on R.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical patients X and Y score 30/95 and 95/30 percent on face/object recognition respectively; controls score 95/95. Describe the dissociation and the inference. Give one limitation.
questions.explanation: X shows relatively selective face impairment; Y shows the opposite pattern. Together this is a double dissociation. It supports at least partially distinct resources rather than one fixed ordering of task difficulty. It does not prove completely independent modules; sensory demands, lesion extent, baseline ability, and network effects need evaluation.
rubric: X shows relatively selective face impairment; Y shows the opposite pattern.
Together this is a double dissociation.
It supports at least partially distinct resources rather than one fixed ordering of task difficulty.
It does not prove completely independent modules; sensory demands, lesion extent, baseline ability, and network effects need evaluation.
commonMistakes: One patient alone could reflect unequal task difficulty. The opposite pattern in a second patient challenges a simple fixed ordering, but it still does not demonstrate completely independent face and object modules.

questions.prompt: An fMRI contrast shows FFA prefers faces over houses and PPA prefers houses over faces. State what this supports, what it does not establish, and a follow-up test.
questions.explanation: It supports differentiated task/stimulus selectivity across regions. It is correlational evidence of involvement. It does not show either region is exclusively sufficient or necessary for recognition. Lesion evidence or a feasible controlled perturbation can test causal contributions, with matched visual/task controls.
rubric: It supports differentiated task/stimulus selectivity across regions.
It is correlational evidence of involvement.
It does not show either region is exclusively sufficient or necessary for recognition.
Lesion evidence or a feasible controlled perturbation can test causal contributions, with matched visual/task controls.
commonMistakes: A crossed activation preference is not proof that either area is necessary or exclusively devoted to its preferred category. A causal follow-up must alter or examine damage to the system and control alternative task demands.

questions.prompt: Design a controlled TMS test of a candidate region's role in visual attention. Include site, timing, comparison, and outcome interpretation.
questions.explanation: Target an accessible candidate cortical site at a hypothesized processing time. Compare sham/control-site and control-time stimulation. Measure attention performance while controlling nonspecific effects and basic vision/motor demands. A selective disruption supports a causal contribution under those conditions, not a sole brain location for all attention.
rubric: Target an accessible candidate cortical site at a hypothesized processing time.
Compare sham/control-site and control-time stimulation.
Measure attention performance while controlling nonspecific effects and basic vision/motor demands.
A selective disruption supports a causal contribution under those conditions, not a sole brain location for all attention.
commonMistakes: A performance drop after stimulation could reflect sound, discomfort, distraction, or motor effects. Site, timing, sham/control conditions, and matched tasks are needed before attributing the change specifically to attention processing.

questions.prompt: Trace the main visual pathway from photoreceptors to V1 and then into the two broad cortical streams. Identify the thalamic relay and describe changes in representation.
questions.explanation: Rods/cones -> bipolar cells -> retinal ganglion cells. Ganglion axons -> optic nerve/pathway -> LGN of thalamus -> V1. V1 supplies downstream ventral temporal identity and dorsal parietal spatial/action processing. Representations progress from local contrast/edges toward more complex properties, often with larger receptive fields; the system also has feedback and parallel paths.
rubric: Rods/cones -> bipolar cells -> retinal ganglion cells.
Ganglion axons -> optic nerve/pathway -> LGN of thalamus -> V1.
V1 supplies downstream ventral temporal identity and dorsal parietal spatial/action processing.
Representations progress from local contrast/edges toward more complex properties, often with larger receptive fields; the system also has feedback and parallel paths.
commonMistakes: Do not place ganglion cells before bipolar cells or V1 before the main thalamic relay. Dorsal and ventral processing are downstream broad streams, not a claim that the whole visual system is strictly linear and has no feedback.

questions.prompt: Define a receptive field. Describe how you would map a neuron's receptive field and distinguish that from measuring its tuning curve.
questions.explanation: A receptive field is the part of sensory space where stimulation alters a neuron's response, with relevant stimulus properties specified. Present controlled stimuli at many positions while recording spikes against baseline. Identify excitatory/inhibitory locations and response pattern. A tuning curve then varies a feature such as orientation while holding location/other variables controlled.
rubric: A receptive field is the part of sensory space where stimulation alters a neuron's response, with relevant stimulus properties specified.
Present controlled stimuli at many positions while recording spikes against baseline.
Identify excitatory/inhibitory locations and response pattern.
A tuning curve then varies a feature such as orientation while holding location/other variables controlled.
commonMistakes: A receptive field describes where stimulation changes the response; a tuning curve describes sensitivity to a feature value such as orientation. Varying location and orientation together confounds those two measurements.

questions.prompt: Predict the response of an ON-center/OFF-surround cell to center-only light, surround-only light, uniform illumination, and the contrast-reversed OFF-center case.
questions.explanation: Center-only light increases ON-center firing. Surround-only light suppresses it relative to baseline. Uniform light produces opposing effects/partial cancellation and typically less response than isolated center illumination. An OFF-center/ON-surround cell has reversed polarity and responds strongly to a dark center against an illuminated surround.
rubric: Center-only light increases ON-center firing.
Surround-only light suppresses it relative to baseline.
Uniform light produces opposing effects/partial cancellation and typically less response than isolated center illumination.
An OFF-center/ON-surround cell has reversed polarity and responds strongly to a dark center against an illuminated surround.
commonMistakes: ON-center does not mean every light anywhere increases firing. The surround has the opposing effect, and reversing ON/OFF polarity reverses which center-surround contrast is preferred; suppression is relative to baseline, not negative spike counts.

questions.prompt: Explain how an edge can produce different firing rates in neighboring center-surround cells even when a uniformly illuminated surface produces little contrast signal.
questions.explanation: Center and surround have antagonistic effects. Over a uniform surface, both regions receive similar light, partly canceling. Near an edge, center and surround can sample different luminances. Unequal excitation/inhibition creates a response pattern emphasizing contrast rather than merely total light.
rubric: Center and surround have antagonistic effects.
Over a uniform surface, both regions receive similar light, partly canceling.
Near an edge, center and surround can sample different luminances.
Unequal excitation/inhibition creates a response pattern emphasizing contrast rather than merely total light.
commonMistakes: More total light does not necessarily yield a stronger contrast response. The important comparison is the luminance reaching center versus surround, so a uniformly bright area can evoke less response than a boundary.

questions.prompt: A neuron fires at 5, 20, 60, 25, and 6 spikes/s for bars at 0, 30, 60, 90, and 120 degrees. Describe its tuning curve and identify what can and cannot be concluded.
questions.explanation: Describe orientation on the x-axis and firing rate on the y-axis, with the highest tested response at 60 degrees. The neuron is tuned to orientation with strongest tested response at 60 degrees. It also responds to other tested orientations; preference does not imply exclusivity. The data alone do not establish identity of an entire perceived object, the cell's anatomical location, or responses to untested orientations.
rubric: Describe orientation on the x-axis and firing rate on the y-axis, with the highest tested response at 60 degrees.
The neuron is tuned to orientation with strongest tested response at 60 degrees.
It also responds to other tested orientations; preference does not imply exclusivity.
The data alone do not establish identity of an entire perceived object, the cell's anatomical location, or responses to untested orientations.
commonMistakes: The maximum tested response at 60 degrees is a preference, not proof of an exclusive detector. Positive responses at other tested orientations and untested angles rule out claiming that the cell responds only at 60 degrees.

questions.prompt: Contrast dorsal and ventral streams in destination, typical information, and a behavioral dissociation. Avoid calling them fully independent.
questions.explanation: Ventral processing extends toward temporal regions and emphasizes identity/form. Dorsal processing extends toward parietal regions and emphasizes space/visually guided action. Preserved identification with impaired visually guided reaching, or the reverse pattern, supports differentiated contributions. They interact and tasks recruit broader systems; labels are useful simplifications.
rubric: Ventral processing extends toward temporal regions and emphasizes identity/form.
Dorsal processing extends toward parietal regions and emphasizes space/visually guided action.
Preserved identification with impaired visually guided reaching, or the reverse pattern, supports differentiated contributions.
They interact and tasks recruit broader systems; labels are useful simplifications.
commonMistakes: Dorsal is not the identity stream and ventral is not the main action/spatial comparison. A behavioral dissociation supports differentiated contributions without showing that the two streams never communicate or share processing.

questions.prompt: Explain the binding problem using a red moving car. Why does knowing that neurons code color, motion, and shape separately not yet explain a unified percept?
questions.explanation: Different neural populations can encode different features. The system must assign features to the correct object rather than combine them arbitrarily. A unified percept requires linking this redness, motion, and shape to the same car. Attention/spatial correspondence and interactions among representations help constrain binding; one feature detector alone cannot solve object assignment.
rubric: Different neural populations can encode different features.
The system must assign features to the correct object rather than combine them arbitrarily.
A unified percept requires linking this redness, motion, and shape to the same car.
Attention/spatial correspondence and interactions among representations help constrain binding; one feature detector alone cannot solve object assignment.
commonMistakes: Listing separate color, motion, and shape detectors only restates the problem. Binding must explain why these features belong to this car rather than to other simultaneously visible objects.

questions.prompt: Distinguish a ganglion-cell contrast response, a V1 edge/orientation response, and downstream object selectivity. Explain why increasingly complex responses do not require a single unique neuron for every object.
questions.explanation: Retinal ganglion center-surround organization emphasizes local luminance contrast. V1 neurons can respond selectively to oriented edges/bars. Downstream populations can represent more complex shapes/objects and broader receptive fields. Population/sparse codes can combine selective responses; selective firing does not imply one unique neuron exclusively stores each object.
rubric: Retinal ganglion center-surround organization emphasizes local luminance contrast.
V1 neurons can respond selectively to oriented edges/bars.
Downstream populations can represent more complex shapes/objects and broader receptive fields.
Population/sparse codes can combine selective responses; selective firing does not imply one unique neuron exclusively stores each object.
commonMistakes: Increasing feature complexity does not require a unique neuron that stores each whole object alone. Selective neurons can contribute to overlapping sparse or population patterns, so selectivity does not establish exclusivity or necessity.

questions.prompt: Define bottom-up and top-down processing. Give a case in which both influence the same ambiguous stimulus and state a limitation of top-down processing.
questions.explanation: Bottom-up processing builds from sensory input/features. Top-down processing uses context, expectations, or knowledge. An ambiguous letter/digit can be resolved differently in word versus number context despite identical shape. Expectations can bias errors and remain constrained by sensory evidence; they are not proof that perception ignores the world.
rubric: Bottom-up processing builds from sensory input/features.
Top-down processing uses context, expectations, or knowledge.
An ambiguous letter/digit can be resolved differently in word versus number context despite identical shape.
Expectations can bias errors and remain constrained by sensory evidence; they are not proof that perception ignores the world.
commonMistakes: Top-down influence does not make sensory input irrelevant. Context can bias an ambiguous shape, but the remaining bottom-up evidence constrains which readings are plausible and can sometimes override an expectation.

questions.prompt: Explain proximity, similarity, good continuation, and closure with one concrete grouping example each.
questions.explanation: Nearby dots group by proximity. Items with shared shape/color group by similarity. Smoothly aligned segments group as a continuing contour. Incomplete contours may be perceived as closed figures. Accurate examples earn credit; grouping principles describe tendencies, not guarantees.
rubric: Nearby dots group by proximity.
Items with shared shape/color group by similarity.
Smoothly aligned segments group as a continuing contour.
Incomplete contours may be perceived as closed figures. Accurate examples earn credit; grouping principles describe tendencies, not guarantees.
commonMistakes: Keep the grouping cues distinct: proximity is spatial nearness, similarity is shared appearance, continuation is smooth alignment, and closure bridges incomplete boundaries. A single example should illustrate the intended cue rather than relabel a different one.

questions.prompt: Explain common fate and figure-ground organization. Describe how they could help identify an animal partly hidden in leaves.
questions.explanation: Elements moving together can group by common fate. Figure-ground organization distinguishes a bounded object from its background. Coordinated movement of visible animal patches supports a single object. Assigning contours/regions to animal versus foliage supports segmentation even when input is incomplete.
rubric: Elements moving together can group by common fate.
Figure-ground organization distinguishes a bounded object from its background.
Coordinated movement of visible animal patches supports a single object.
Assigning contours/regions to animal versus foliage supports segmentation even when input is incomplete.
commonMistakes: Common fate concerns coordinated motion, not simply similar color. Figure-ground organization concerns assigning regions and borders to object versus background; neither requires every part of the animal to be visible.

questions.prompt: Classify and explain binocular disparity, interposition, linear perspective, and motion parallax as depth cues.
questions.explanation: Binocular disparity compares the two eyes' different views. Interposition is monocular: the occluding object is typically nearer. Linear perspective is monocular: parallel lines project toward convergence with distance. Motion parallax is monocular over movement: nearer objects change visual position more rapidly than distant objects relative to the observer.
rubric: Binocular disparity compares the two eyes' different views.
Interposition is monocular: the occluding object is typically nearer.
Linear perspective is monocular: parallel lines project toward convergence with distance.
Motion parallax is monocular over movement: nearer objects change visual position more rapidly than distant objects relative to the observer.
commonMistakes: Motion parallax uses changes over observer movement and does not require comparing two eyes. Binocular disparity is the two-eye comparison; perspective, occlusion, and texture information can be available in a single view.

questions.prompt: A friend walks away but seems roughly the same size. A door rotates yet seems rectangular. Explain both constancies and distinguish retinal input from inferred object properties.
questions.explanation: The friend's retinal image shrinks with distance. Size constancy uses distance/context to support stable perceived object size. The rotating door changes its retinal projection. Shape constancy supports a stable interpretation of the object's shape despite viewpoint change. Constancy is approximate and can fail in misleading contexts.
rubric: The friend's retinal image shrinks with distance.
Size constancy uses distance/context to support stable perceived object size.
The rotating door changes its retinal projection.
Shape constancy supports a stable interpretation of the object's shape despite viewpoint change. Constancy is approximate and can fail in misleading contexts.
commonMistakes: Constancy does not mean the retinal image stays unchanged. It means perceived object properties remain relatively stable despite image changes; misleading depth or context can make that compensation inaccurate.

questions.prompt: Describe a feature net from elementary features to letters and words. Explain threshold, converging evidence, and why recognition need not wait for perfect input.
questions.explanation: Low-level feature detectors feed candidate letter representations and then word representations. A detector responds when accumulated activation reaches its threshold. Multiple compatible features/candidates can contribute converging evidence; frequent/primed detectors can be easier to activate. Partial input can therefore yield recognition, with a risk of a plausible but wrong winner.
rubric: Low-level feature detectors feed candidate letter representations and then word representations.
A detector responds when accumulated activation reaches its threshold.
Multiple compatible features/candidates can contribute converging evidence; frequent/primed detectors can be easier to activate.
Partial input can therefore yield recognition, with a risk of a plausible but wrong winner.
commonMistakes: A recognition threshold is not a requirement for a perfect image. Accumulated, partly matching evidence can activate a candidate, and that same tolerance explains how a plausible incorrect candidate can win.

questions.prompt: Explain how a feature net can resolve ambiguity, produce a familiar-word error, and show priming. State what an error reveals about the system.
questions.explanation: Context and accumulated feature evidence favor some candidates over others. A familiar expected candidate can reach threshold despite mismatching/incomplete input. Recent exposure or expectation can preactivate relevant detectors/lower effective recognition demands. Errors reveal constructive, evidence-weighted inference rather than literal copying of the retinal image.
rubric: Context and accumulated feature evidence favor some candidates over others.
A familiar expected candidate can reach threshold despite mismatching/incomplete input.
Recent exposure or expectation can preactivate relevant detectors/lower effective recognition demands.
Errors reveal constructive, evidence-weighted inference rather than literal copying of the retinal image.
commonMistakes: An error is not proof that no features were processed. Feature evidence, prior activation, and context can jointly favor the wrong familiar candidate; that pattern is informative about how recognition is constructed.

questions.prompt: Compare Recognition by Components with a simple feature net. Include geons, spatial relations, a shared principle, and a difference.
questions.explanation: RBC identifies volumetric components called geons. Their spatial arrangement distinguishes objects composed of similar parts. Both accounts build complex recognition from combinations of simpler elements. RBC emphasizes three-dimensional component structure and relations rather than only a simple feature-to-letter/word hierarchy.
rubric: RBC identifies volumetric components called geons.
Their spatial arrangement distinguishes objects composed of similar parts.
Both accounts build complex recognition from combinations of simpler elements.
RBC emphasizes three-dimensional component structure and relations rather than only a simple feature-to-letter/word hierarchy.
commonMistakes: Geons are volumetric components, not merely any flat letter feature. Listing parts without their relations cannot distinguish objects made from the same components arranged differently.

questions.prompt: Design a recognition experiment that contrasts viewpoint-dependent predictions with RBC-style structural predictions. State an important qualification.
questions.explanation: Show learned objects from familiar and novel viewpoints while measuring accuracy/latency. A viewpoint-dependent account predicts costs as views depart from learned appearances. RBC predicts relative robustness across views preserving diagnostic components/relations. Views that hide diagnostic geons can harm RBC too; viewpoint effects alone do not establish one universal recognition mechanism.
rubric: Show learned objects from familiar and novel viewpoints while measuring accuracy/latency.
A viewpoint-dependent account predicts costs as views depart from learned appearances.
RBC predicts relative robustness across views preserving diagnostic components/relations.
Views that hide diagnostic geons can harm RBC too; viewpoint effects alone do not establish one universal recognition mechanism.
commonMistakes: Novel-view costs alone do not automatically disprove RBC. If a view hides diagnostic components, even a structural account predicts difficulty; preserve or manipulate component visibility to separate the predictions.

questions.prompt: Explain what may be special about face recognition using configural processing, inversion, and prosopagnosia. Give one reason to avoid claiming faces and objects share no processing at all.
questions.explanation: Face identity depends strongly on relationships among similar parts/configuration. Face inversion often disproportionately impairs this processing. Prosopagnosia can impair familiar face recognition despite some preserved other visual abilities. Faces still share visual features/resources with objects, and expertise/task demands matter; a dissociation does not establish zero overlap.
rubric: Face identity depends strongly on relationships among similar parts/configuration.
Face inversion often disproportionately impairs this processing.
Prosopagnosia can impair familiar face recognition despite some preserved other visual abilities.
