Faces still share visual features/resources with objects, and expertise/task demands matter; a dissociation does not establish zero overlap.
commonMistakes: Configural processing does not mean faces have no features. Inversion and prosopagnosia support differentiated processing, but neither establishes zero overlap between face and object recognition or eliminates expertise-related alternatives.

questions.prompt: Compare strict early selection, late selection, and attenuation by selection stage and the fate of unattended input. Give an outcome that would challenge complete presemantic filtering, and explain why it would not uniquely prove late selection.
questions.explanation: Strict early selection filters on physical/channel properties before full semantic interpretation. Late selection allows meaning analysis before selection for response or awareness. Attenuation weakens rather than erases unattended input; unequal thresholds allow especially salient items to break through. A semantic effect from nominally unattended material, such as meaning-dependent interference or own-name detection, challenges complete exclusion before meaning analysis. Such an effect is compatible with later selection but can also reflect attenuation or a brief attention shift. A stronger test controls attention shifts and separates semantic processing from conscious report.
rubric: Strict early selection filters on physical/channel properties before full semantic interpretation.
Late selection allows meaning analysis before selection for response or awareness.
Attenuation weakens rather than erases unattended input; unequal thresholds allow especially salient items to break through.
A semantic effect from nominally unattended material, such as meaning-dependent interference or own-name detection, challenges complete exclusion before meaning analysis.

Such an effect is compatible with later selection but can also reflect attenuation or a brief attention shift. A stronger test controls attention shifts and separates semantic processing from conscious report.
commonMistakes: Name detection does not uniquely prove that every unattended word underwent full late selection. Attenuation with low thresholds or a brief attention shift can also produce meaningful breakthrough and require separate controls.

questions.prompt: In dichotic listening, people shadow one ear, detect physical changes in the other, but recall few unattended words. Occasionally their name breaks through. Explain evidence for early filtering and the challenge to a strict version.
questions.explanation: Shadowing concentrates processing on the selected channel. Preserved detection of voice/physical changes with poor word report supports physical-channel selection. Detection of a meaningful name challenges complete presemantic exclusion. Attenuation/threshold differences or occasional attention shifts must be distinguished experimentally; name detection alone does not prove full semantic processing of every unattended word.
rubric: Shadowing concentrates processing on the selected channel.
Preserved detection of voice/physical changes with poor word report supports physical-channel selection.
Detection of a meaningful name challenges complete presemantic exclusion.
Attenuation/threshold differences or occasional attention shifts must be distinguished experimentally; name detection alone does not prove full semantic processing of every unattended word.
commonMistakes: Poor later recall of unattended words is not proof of absolutely no processing, and noticing one's name is not proof of full conscious processing of every word. Distinguish physical-change detection, semantic influence, and report.

questions.prompt: Separate stimulus-driven and expectation-based priming in direction, effort, predictive-cue sensitivity, and costs to unexpected targets.
questions.explanation: Stimulus-driven priming reflects activation caused by input/recent related stimulation. Expectation-based priming reflects top-down preparation for predicted stimuli. In the course model, expectation-based preparation uses limited resources/effort and depends on cue predictiveness. Stimulus-driven facilitation is described as cost-free, whereas misallocated expectation can impair unexpected items relative to neutral baseline.
rubric: Stimulus-driven priming reflects activation caused by input/recent related stimulation.
Expectation-based priming reflects top-down preparation for predicted stimuli.
In the course model, expectation-based preparation uses limited resources/effort and depends on cue predictiveness.
Stimulus-driven facilitation is described as cost-free, whereas misallocated expectation can impair unexpected items relative to neutral baseline.
commonMistakes: Both forms can speed responses, so a benefit alone does not identify expectation. In the course account, cue predictiveness and costs to unexpected stimuli help distinguish resource-demanding preparation from cost-free stimulus-driven facilitation.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical mean RTs are: low-validity valid 470, neutral 500, invalid 500 ms; high-validity valid 420, neutral 500, invalid 550 ms. Compute valid benefits and invalid costs and interpret.
questions.explanation: Low-validity valid benefit is 500-470 = 30 ms. Low-validity invalid cost is 500-500 = 0 ms. High-validity benefit is 80 ms and invalid cost is 550-500 = 50 ms. Facilitation without cost fits stimulus-driven priming; added benefit plus invalid cost fits expectation-based allocation. Data are hypothetical, not the original lecture graph.
rubric: Low-validity valid benefit is 500-470 = 30 ms.
Low-validity invalid cost is 500-500 = 0 ms.
High-validity benefit is 80 ms and invalid cost is 550-500 = 50 ms.
Facilitation without cost fits stimulus-driven priming; added benefit plus invalid cost fits expectation-based allocation. Data are hypothetical, not the original lecture graph.
commonMistakes: Calculate each effect against its own neutral baseline: benefit is neutral minus valid, cost is invalid minus neutral. The 130 ms high-validity valid-invalid gap combines an 80 ms benefit and a 50 ms cost.

questions.prompt: Explain why a neutral-cue baseline matters in an attention experiment. Show why a valid-versus-invalid difference alone cannot distinguish benefits from costs.
questions.explanation: A neutral cue estimates performance without a directional expectation. Valid faster than neutral indicates benefit. Invalid slower than neutral indicates cost. A 60 ms valid-invalid gap could reflect benefit alone, cost alone, or both; compare both conditions to neutral and consider accuracy trade-offs.
rubric: A neutral cue estimates performance without a directional expectation.
Valid faster than neutral indicates benefit.
Invalid slower than neutral indicates cost.
A 60 ms valid-invalid gap could reflect benefit alone, cost alone, or both; compare both conditions to neutral and consider accuracy trade-offs.
commonMistakes: A valid-invalid difference is not automatically all a benefit or all a cost. Without neutral trials, the same gap can arise from faster valid responses, slower invalid responses, or both.

questions.prompt: Explain the spotlight analogy and two reasons it is incomplete. Include a Posner cueing result and an object-based result.
questions.explanation: Attention preferentially enhances processing at selected spatial locations, like a spotlight. Faster valid and slower invalid cue responses support spatial prioritization even with fixation. Attention can operate covertly and flexibly rather than being a literal beam with fixed borders. A same-object advantage at equal spatial distance shows selection follows object structure as well as coordinates.
rubric: Attention preferentially enhances processing at selected spatial locations, like a spotlight.
Faster valid and slower invalid cue responses support spatial prioritization even with fixation.
Attention can operate covertly and flexibly rather than being a literal beam with fixed borders.
A same-object advantage at equal spatial distance shows selection follows object structure as well as coordinates.
commonMistakes: The spotlight is an analogy, not a literal beam or a requirement to move the eyes. A same-object advantage at equal distance adds an object-based constraint without eliminating spatial attention.

questions.prompt: In a two-rectangle task, uncued targets are equally distant from the cue. RT is 330 ms on the same rectangle and 370 ms on the other. What is controlled and what inference follows? Give a limitation.
questions.explanation: Cue-target spatial distance is matched across those uncued conditions. Same-object targets are 40 ms faster. This supports object-based prioritization beyond a distance-only account. It does not show spatial attention is absent; stimulus geometry, eye position, and response demands must also be controlled.
rubric: Cue-target spatial distance is matched across those uncued conditions.
Same-object targets are 40 ms faster.
This supports object-based prioritization beyond a distance-only account.
It does not show spatial attention is absent; stimulus geometry, eye position, and response demands must also be controlled.
commonMistakes: Do not attribute the 40 ms same-object advantage simply to a shorter cue-target distance; that distance is matched. The result challenges a distance-only account but still permits spatial and object-based attention to coexist.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical RTs at set sizes 4, 8, 12 are 400, 410, 420 ms for feature search and 450, 550, 650 ms for conjunction search. Compute slopes, interpret, and predict an illusory-conjunction effect under divided attention.
questions.explanation: Feature slope is 20/8 = 2.5 ms/item. Conjunction slope is 200/8 = 25 ms/item. The larger conjunction cost fits attention-demanding feature binding/search in classic FIT. Reduced attention should increase incorrect feature combinations under brief exposure; slopes alone do not prove a strictly serial mechanism in all tasks.
rubric: Feature slope is 20/8 = 2.5 ms/item.
Conjunction slope is 200/8 = 25 ms/item.
The larger conjunction cost fits attention-demanding feature binding/search in classic FIT.
Reduced attention should increase incorrect feature combinations under brief exposure; slopes alone do not prove a strictly serial mechanism in all tasks.
commonMistakes: Divide change in RT by change in set size, not RT by total set size. The resulting 2.5 versus 25 ms/item slopes support the classic contrast but do not prove that every conjunction search uses an invariant serial process.

questions.prompt: A person misses left-side targets after right hemisphere injury. Another person binds colors to the wrong shapes during a brief dual task. Explain how each supports a role for attention without treating the deficits as identical.
questions.explanation: Neglect supports spatially organized attentional selection/representation. Its omissions are often contralesional and not merely primary blindness. Illusory conjunctions show feature detection can be preserved while binding fails. Together they motivate attentional roles in selecting locations/objects and binding features, but they are distinct behaviors/mechanisms.
rubric: Neglect supports spatially organized attentional selection/representation.
Its omissions are often contralesional and not merely primary blindness.
Illusory conjunctions show feature detection can be preserved while binding fails.
Together they motivate attentional roles in selecting locations/objects and binding features, but they are distinct behaviors/mechanisms.
commonMistakes: Neglect and illusory conjunctions are not the same error: one concerns which space is attended, the other which object receives a detected feature. Preserved features can coexist with either attentional problem.

questions.prompt: Distinguish task-general and task-specific resources. Give one kind of evidence for each and explain why a hybrid account can be needed.
questions.explanation: Task-specific resources are shared especially by tasks using similar modalities/codes. Greater interference for two verbal or two spatial tasks supports such pools. Cross-modal interference in response selection/executive control supports task-general limitations. A hybrid explains reduced overlap costs without assuming different modalities eliminate all competition.
rubric: Task-specific resources are shared especially by tasks using similar modalities/codes.
Greater interference for two verbal or two spatial tasks supports such pools.
Cross-modal interference in response selection/executive control supports task-general limitations.
A hybrid explains reduced overlap costs without assuming different modalities eliminate all competition.
commonMistakes: Different modalities do not guarantee no interference, and interference alone does not identify a single universal pool. Similarity effects support specific resources, while cross-modal response/control costs motivate a shared limitation.

questions.prompt: Predict relative dual-task interference for two difficult verbal tasks versus a well-practiced visual tracking task with a simple auditory task. State how similarity, difficulty, and practice affect your prediction.
questions.explanation: Similar verbal tasks compete more for overlapping specific resources. Greater difficulty increases demands and likely interference. Practice can reduce resource demands and improve coordination. The practiced cross-modal pair may interfere less but can still share response-selection/executive bottlenecks; actual task demands matter.
rubric: Similar verbal tasks compete more for overlapping specific resources.
Greater difficulty increases demands and likely interference.
Practice can reduce resource demands and improve coordination.
The practiced cross-modal pair may interfere less but can still share response-selection/executive bottlenecks; actual task demands matter.
commonMistakes: Practice does not guarantee zero interference. Similarity, difficulty, and overlapping response/control demands all matter; compare dual-task performance with each task's own single-task baseline.

questions.prompt: Compare automatic and controlled processes in attention demand, speed/flexibility, learning, and errors when goals change.
questions.explanation: Controlled processing is resource-demanding and goal-directed/flexible. Automatic processing is often fast and low-effort after extensive practice. Practice can shift performance toward automaticity but does not guarantee no resource use. Automatic habits can intrude after a rule change; controlled inhibition/switching may be needed, as in perseveration/Stroop-like conflict.
rubric: Controlled processing is resource-demanding and goal-directed/flexible.
Automatic processing is often fast and low-effort after extensive practice.
Practice can shift performance toward automaticity but does not guarantee no resource use.
Automatic habits can intrude after a rule change; controlled inhibition/switching may be needed, as in perseveration/Stroop-like conflict.
commonMistakes: Automatic is not synonymous with infallible or completely resource-free. A learned response can intrude when goals change, whereas controlled processing is more flexible but demands limited attention.

questions.prompt: Design a 2 x 2 dual-task study that can test task similarity and practice. Specify factors, outcome, prediction, and one control.
questions.explanation: Cross similar versus dissimilar secondary task with practiced versus unpracticed primary task. Measure dual-task costs relative to single-task baselines using RT and accuracy. Predict larger costs for similar/unpracticed combinations and reduced costs after practice. Match baseline difficulty or account for it, counterbalance order, and avoid interpreting a speed-accuracy trade-off as improvement. One suitable control suffices for the final point.
rubric: Cross similar versus dissimilar secondary task with practiced versus unpracticed primary task.
Measure dual-task costs relative to single-task baselines using RT and accuracy.
Predict larger costs for similar/unpracticed combinations and reduced costs after practice.
Match baseline difficulty or account for it, counterbalance order, and avoid interpreting a speed-accuracy trade-off as improvement. One suitable control suffices for the final point.
commonMistakes: Two conditions alone are not a full 2 x 2 design. Cross both similarity levels with both practice levels, and measure costs relative to single-task baselines so easier tasks or speed-accuracy trade-offs do not mimic a practice benefit.

flashcards.question: How does cognitive psychology differ from strict behaviorism?
flashcards.answer: Cognitive psychology uses measurable behavior to infer internal representations and processes. Strict behaviorism focuses on observable stimulus–response relations and sets aside mental-process explanations.

flashcards.question: What is a mental process, and why is a brain scan alone insufficient to identify it?
flashcards.answer: A mental process transforms, selects, stores, retrieves, or uses information. Activation identifies a neural correlate; different computations can produce similar activation, so behavioral predictions and comparisons matter.

flashcards.question: What is the transcendental method, and how does mental rotation illustrate it?
flashcards.answer: Work backward from observable effects to infer hidden processes that could produce them. Increasing response time with angular disparity supports a mental-rotation account. It does not directly reveal a thought or establish a unique mechanism.

flashcards.question: What is a limitation of introspection?
flashcards.answer: Reports of conscious experience are difficult to verify independently and do not reveal every unconscious process. Cognitive experiments use controlled behavior to constrain explanations.

flashcards.question: How are CNS/PNS and afferent/efferent organized?
flashcards.answer: CNS: brain and spinal cord. PNS: neural structures outside the CNS. Afferent input travels toward the CNS; efferent output travels away. Somatic pathways serve bodily sensation/skeletal muscle; autonomic pathways regulate organs and glands.

flashcards.question: What do the main forebrain direction terms mean?
flashcards.answer: Dorsal = top; ventral = bottom. Anterior/rostral = front; posterior/caudal = back. Medial = toward the midline; lateral = away. Ipsilateral = same side; contralateral = opposite side.

flashcards.question: Where are the four cerebral lobes, and what are their broad roles?
flashcards.answer: Frontal: anterior, motor/executive functions. Parietal: upper posterior cerebrum, somatosensory/spatial processing. Temporal: lateral/inferior, hearing/recognition and memory-related systems. Occipital: posterior, vision. These functions are not exclusive.

flashcards.question: Which sulci locate motor, somatosensory, and temporal cortex?
flashcards.answer: Primary motor cortex is just anterior to the central sulcus; primary somatosensory cortex is just posterior. The lateral sulcus separates temporal cortex below from frontal/parietal cortex above.

flashcards.question: How do thalamus and hypothalamus differ?
flashcards.answer: The thalamus is deep near the midline and relays much sensory information to cortex. The hypothalamus lies below it and supports homeostasis and endocrine regulation, including hunger, thirst, and temperature.

flashcards.question: Where are hippocampus and amygdala, and what do they contribute?
flashcards.answer: Both lie in medial temporal regions. Hippocampus, posterior to amygdala, supports new learning and memory formation. Amygdala contributes to threat and other emotional processing; neither is the sole location of memory or emotion.

flashcards.question: Distinguish apraxia, agnosia, aphasia, and neglect.
flashcards.answer: Apraxia: impaired learned purposeful action beyond simple weakness. Agnosia: impaired recognition despite sufficient sensation. Aphasia: language impairment. Neglect: reduced attention/response to contralesional space, commonly left space after right-hemisphere injury.

flashcards.question: How do primary and association areas differ, and why is the hand large on cortical maps?
flashcards.answer: Primary areas have sensory/motor maps: motor just anterior to the central sulcus in frontal cortex; somatosensory just posterior in parietal cortex; visual in occipital cortex; auditory in temporal cortex. Association areas integrate and interpret information. Map size reflects sensitivity or motor precision, not body-part size.

flashcards.question: Trace a typical neuron's information flow.
flashcards.answer: Dendrites/soma receive input; integration near the axon hillock/initial segment determines firing; the axon conducts action potentials; terminals release transmitter. Myelin promotes rapid, reliable conduction.

flashcards.question: How do postsynaptic potentials differ from action potentials?
flashcards.answer: Postsynaptic potentials are graded and can sum across space and time. Action potentials are approximately all-or-none and regenerate along axons. Stronger input usually changes firing probability/rate rather than spike height.

flashcards.question: What determines whether a synapse is excitatory or inhibitory?
flashcards.answer: The effect on the postsynaptic cell's probability of reaching firing threshold. Receptor type, ion conductances, and ionic conditions matter; transmitter identity alone does not uniquely determine the effect.

flashcards.question: What crosses a typical chemical synapse?
flashcards.answer: The presynaptic action potential triggers transmitter release. Transmitter diffuses through the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors, changing postsynaptic electrical activity. The action potential itself does not jump across the cleft.

flashcards.question: What is the main EEG–fMRI tradeoff?
flashcards.answer: EEG records scalp electrical population activity with millisecond timing but limited source localization. fMRI measures indirect BOLD changes with finer spatial localization but slow hemodynamic timing.

flashcards.question: Why can TMS support a causal claim?
flashcards.answer: TMS perturbs an accessible cortical site while performance is measured. Selective disruption versus sham/control sites or times supports a causal contribution; nonspecific sound, sensation, and task demands require controls.

flashcards.question: What is reverse inference?
flashcards.answer: Inferring a particular mental process because a region associated with it is active. The region may participate in other processes; selectivity, base rates, and alternatives matter. Activation alone also fails to establish necessity.

flashcards.question: What does a double dissociation support?
flashcards.answer: One patient is impaired on A but relatively spared on B; another shows the reverse. This supports differentiated resources and challenges a simple fixed task-difficulty account. It does not prove completely independent modules.

flashcards.question: Trace the main retinal pathway to primary visual cortex.
flashcards.answer: Rods/cones → bipolar cells → retinal ganglion cells → optic nerve/pathway → lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus → V1. Ganglion-cell axons form the optic nerve.

flashcards.question: What does each main retinal cell stage contribute?
flashcards.answer: Photoreceptors transduce light into neural signals. Bipolar cells relay within the retina. Ganglion cells send output to the brain; their center–surround responses emphasize local contrast.

flashcards.question: How does a receptive field differ from a tuning curve?
flashcards.answer: A receptive field specifies where sensory stimulation changes a neuron's response. A tuning curve measures response across a feature dimension, such as orientation, with location and other conditions controlled.

flashcards.question: What best excites an ON-center/OFF-surround cell?
flashcards.answer: Light in the center with a dark surround. Surround-only light suppresses firing; uniform illumination partly cancels center and surround effects. OFF-center/ON-surround cells have reversed polarity.

flashcards.question: Where do dorsal and ventral visual streams lead?
flashcards.answer: Dorsal processing extends toward parietal cortex and emphasizes spatial/action information. Ventral processing extends toward temporal cortex and emphasizes identity/form. They interact rather than working as fully isolated systems.

flashcards.question: How do bottom-up and top-down processing interact?
flashcards.answer: Bottom-up processing uses stimulus features; top-down processing uses expectations, context, and knowledge. Context can resolve an ambiguous letter/digit but can also bias errors; sensory evidence still constrains interpretation.

flashcards.question: What do the main Gestalt grouping principles predict?
flashcards.answer: Proximity groups nearby elements; similarity groups shared features; good continuation groups aligned contours; closure completes interrupted shapes; common fate groups common movement. Figure–ground organization separates an object from its background.

flashcards.question: Which depth cues are binocular versus monocular?
flashcards.answer: Binocular disparity compares the eyes' images. Interposition, linear perspective, texture gradient, and motion parallax can provide depth with one eye; motion parallax uses changes as the observer moves.

flashcards.question: What are size and shape constancy?
flashcards.answer: Size constancy preserves approximate perceived object size despite distance-related retinal shrinkage. Shape constancy preserves approximate object shape despite viewpoint changes. Both use context and can fail under misleading conditions.

flashcards.question: How can a feature net recognize incomplete input and make errors?
flashcards.answer: Feature evidence activates candidate letters/words. Converging evidence and priming can bring a detector to threshold before all details are available; familiar or expected candidates can therefore win incorrectly.

flashcards.question: What does Recognition by Components propose?
flashcards.answer: Objects are represented through volumetric components called geons and their spatial relations. Many viewpoints preserve diagnostic components, supporting recognition; views that hide them can still cause difficulty.

flashcards.question: What do inversion and prosopagnosia suggest about faces?
flashcards.answer: Face recognition relies strongly on configuration and relations among parts. Inversion often disrupts it disproportionately; prosopagnosia can impair familiar-face recognition. These findings do not imply zero overlap with object processing.

flashcards.question: How would you contrast viewpoint-dependent and RBC predictions?
flashcards.answer: Test familiar and novel views. Viewpoint-dependent recognition predicts costs away from learned views. RBC predicts relative stability when diagnostic geons and relations remain visible; hidden components are an important qualification.

flashcards.question: Compare early selection, late selection, and attenuation.
flashcards.answer: Strict early selection filters physical characteristics before full meaning analysis. Late selection allows more semantic analysis before response/awareness selection. Attenuation weakens unattended input. Semantic effects from unattended material challenge a complete early filter, but can also reflect attenuation or attention shifts.

flashcards.question: How do stimulus-driven and expectation-based priming differ?
flashcards.answer: Stimulus-driven priming follows input or recent activation and is described as cost-free in the course model. Expectation-based priming allocates limited resources to predicted input, producing valid benefits and possible invalid costs.

flashcards.question: Why include a neutral-cue baseline?
flashcards.answer: Valid faster than neutral measures benefit; invalid slower than neutral measures cost. A valid–invalid difference alone cannot reveal how much comes from facilitation versus impairment. Compare accuracy as well as response time.

flashcards.question: What is the classic FIT prediction for feature and conjunction search?
flashcards.answer: Single distinctive features can pop out with little set-size cost. Conjunction search has larger set-size costs because attention binds features at locations. Under brief/divided attention, features can be combined incorrectly as illusory conjunctions.

flashcards.question: What shows attention is both spatial and object-based?
flashcards.answer: Valid spatial cues improve performance even without eye movements. In two-object tasks, an uncued target on the cued object can be faster than an equally distant target on another object. Object structure adds to spatial prioritization.

flashcards.question: Why can different-modality tasks still interfere?
flashcards.answer: They may share task-general executive or response-selection resources even when task-specific sensory/code resources overlap less. Similarity and difficulty increase competition; practice can reduce demands without eliminating every bottleneck.

flashcards.question: How do automatic and controlled processes differ?
flashcards.answer: Controlled processing demands attention and is flexible/goal-directed. Automatic processing is often fast and low-effort after practice but can intrude when goals change. Automaticity does not guarantee zero resource use.

108.title: PSYC 108 Midterm 1
108.scope: Midterm 1: neuroanatomy, methods, concept coding, and dissociations

questions.prompt: Cognitive neuroscience primarily investigates:
questions.explanation: It connects cognitive questions with neural mechanisms using multiple kinds of evidence.
choices: The relationship between brain structure/function and mental processes.
Only introspective reports.
Only the shape of the skull.
Only computer performance without human evidence.
choiceExplanations: Cognitive neuroscience links questions about cognition to the brain systems and neural mechanisms that support it, using behavioral and neural evidence.
Introspection can provide reports, but it is not the field's sole evidence. Neural measurements, behavior, and causal interventions also contribute.
Skull shape does not specify the field's subject or validly identify cognitive functions. The relevant relationship concerns brain systems and mental processes.
Computational models can test candidate mechanisms, but computer performance alone is not the whole of cognitive neuroscience or sufficient evidence about humans.

questions.prompt: The yellow connection links left frontal cortex with left parietal cortex. It is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Association fibers connect cortical regions within one hemisphere. Crossing hemispheres would indicate commissural fibers.
choices: A commissural tract.
An association tract.
A projection tract.
A ventricle.
choiceExplanations: Commissural fibers connect the hemispheres. Both endpoints here are in the left hemisphere, so this is not the defining commissural arrangement.
An association tract connects cortical regions within the same hemisphere. Left frontal and left parietal cortex meet both parts of that definition.
Projection pathways connect cortex with subcortical or spinal levels. This example instead has two cortical endpoints in one hemisphere.
A ventricle is a CSF-filled cavity, not a bundle of axons connecting cortical regions.

questions.prompt: Which structure most directly fits a broad role in endocrine-linked regulation of hunger, thirst, and temperature?
questions.explanation: Hypothalamus supports homeostatic/endocrine regulation; thalamus is primarily the sensory-relay comparison.
choices: Hippocampus.
Occipital cortex.
Hypothalamus.
Corpus callosum.
choiceExplanations: The hippocampus is important for new learning and memory. It is not the best match for the endocrine/homeostatic regulation described.
Occipital cortex is broadly associated with visual processing. Hunger, thirst, temperature, and endocrine regulation point to a different system.
The hypothalamus links neural and endocrine regulation and helps maintain bodily conditions, making it the best fit for this collection of functions.
The corpus callosum is a commissural connection between cerebral hemispheres. It is not the principal homeostatic/endocrine regulator.

questions.prompt: Which contrast is most accurate?
questions.explanation: Both participate in motor systems, but their broad roles differ; neither alone accounts for all motor behavior.
choices: Basal ganglia produce all movement, while cerebellum only stores words.
Cerebellum is a ventricle, while basal ganglia are white matter tracts.
Both are simply primary visual cortex.
Basal ganglia contribute to action regulation and habit/reward learning; cerebellum contributes to coordination and sensory-feedback integration.
choiceExplanations: Movement depends on many interacting systems. The basal ganglia do not produce all movement, and the cerebellum is not merely a word-storage structure.
The cerebellum is neural tissue rather than a CSF cavity. Basal ganglia include deep gray-matter nuclei, not simply white-matter tracts.
Primary visual cortex is cortical tissue in occipital regions. Neither the basal ganglia nor the cerebellum is another name for it.
This distinguishes broad contributions to action regulation and learning from coordination and feedback integration. Both participate in broader motor networks.

questions.prompt: Scalp EEG primarily reflects:
questions.explanation: Population postsynaptic currents, especially from aligned pyramidal neurons, contribute to the recorded scalp voltages.
choices: Summed postsynaptic electrical activity of suitably aligned cortical populations.
Blood oxygenation inside deep nuclei only.
A static image of axon anatomy.
One action potential from every neuron separately.
choiceExplanations: Scalp potentials largely reflect summed postsynaptic activity from suitably aligned populations, especially cortical pyramidal cells. EEG is a population electrical measurement.
Blood-oxygenation changes are hemodynamic measurements, associated with methods such as fMRI. EEG records scalp voltages rather than oxygenation only in deep nuclei.
A static anatomical image characterizes structure. EEG instead records a changing electrical signal over time.
Scalp EEG mixes contributions from many sources. It does not isolate a separate spike trace from every individual neuron.

questions.prompt: Which is the best comparison of fMRI and EEG?
questions.explanation: fMRI is a hemodynamic measure with fine spatial resolution and slower dynamics; EEG measures electrical population activity with millisecond timing.
choices: Both have the same signal source and resolution.
fMRI generally offers finer spatial localization; EEG offers finer temporal resolution.
EEG is always surgically invasive.
fMRI directly records every neuron's spike timing.
choiceExplanations: fMRI uses a hemodynamic signal and EEG uses electrical population activity. Different signal sources give them different temporal and spatial limitations.
fMRI generally provides finer spatial localization, whereas EEG follows electrical changes on millisecond scales. The slow vascular response limits fMRI's neural timing.
Standard scalp EEG is noninvasive and does not require surgery. Intracranial recordings are a different acquisition context.
BOLD is an indirect blood-related signal. fMRI does not directly resolve every neuron's action potentials or their precise spike times.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest reason concept-selective single neurons do not establish strict grandmother-cell coding?
questions.explanation: Selectivity and invariance can coexist with distributed population coding. Sampling cannot establish one unique exclusive storage cell.
choices: A selective response means no information was measured.
All brain cells must fire equally for all concepts.
A sampled neuron can be part of a larger sparse population, and untested stimuli/neurons remain unknown.
The studies used only structural MRI.
choiceExplanations: A selective firing response does carry information about tested stimuli. The limitation is the stronger claim of unique, exclusive storage, not an absence of information.
Population coding allows cells to respond differently. It does not require all cells to fire equally for every concept.
Selectivity in one sampled cell is compatible with a sparse ensemble. Limited sampling cannot establish that no other cell represents the concept or no untested stimulus activates this one.
The concept-cell evidence involves invasive single-neuron recordings, not only structural MRI. Mistaking the method does not address the inference limit.

questions.prompt: Quiroga and colleagues' human concept-cell study used:
questions.explanation: Clinically implanted electrodes allowed invasive human recordings, with selection and sampling limitations.
choices: Scalp EEG in healthy infants.
Only functional near-infrared spectroscopy.
A behavioral survey with no brain recording.
Single-neuron recordings from implanted electrodes in epilepsy patients viewing stimuli.
choiceExplanations: The reviewed study used clinical implanted-electrode access in epilepsy patients. Scalp EEG in healthy infants would not be the same population or single-neuron method.
fNIRS estimates blood-related changes with near-infrared light. It does not provide the single-neuron recordings used in this study.
Behavioral surveys do not measure individual neuronal firing. The distinctive evidence here came from actual intracranial neural recordings.
Clinical electrodes allowed researchers to record individual neuronal responses while epilepsy patients viewed stimuli. That access also introduces clinical and sampling limitations.

questions.prompt: A key contribution of Tyree and colleagues' study was evidence for:
questions.explanation: Cross-modal identity coding links different sensory presentations to the same individual; it is not a necessity experiment.
choices: Identity information across faces and voices in primate hippocampal single neurons and population activity.
Only retinal color sensitivity.
The necessity of one isolated cell for all recognition.
The absence of identity information in populations.
choiceExplanations: The reviewed work links hippocampal identity information across faces and voices, examining individual neurons and populations. This tests generalization across sensory modalities.
Retinal color sensitivity concerns early visual processing. It does not explain a hippocampal representation that can relate faces and voices to identity.
Recording selectivity or decoding information is not a test of necessity. Establishing that one cell is required would need causal evidence beyond these responses.
The reviewed population analyses found identity information rather than its absence. Single-cell and population evidence can coexist.

questions.prompt: A patient performs poorly on task A but normally on task B. Why is a single dissociation insufficient to rule out a shared resource?
questions.explanation: A common resource reduced by injury can produce selective impairment if the tasks place unequal demands on it.
choices: It proves neither task can be measured.
Task A may require more of the same resource than task B.
It proves every cortical region is identical.
It eliminates all difficulty differences automatically.
choiceExplanations: A selective impairment does not make the tasks unmeasurable. The question is which resource explanation can generate their different measured outcomes.
If A needs more of a shared resource, a reduction can impair A while leaving enough capacity for B. A single dissociation therefore does not force separate modules.
The result concerns two tasks and does not show that every cortical region has the same structure or function.
Difficulty differences are a potential explanation that must be tested. Observing a dissociation does not automatically control or remove them.

questions.prompt: Gray matter is found only at the outer cerebral cortex.
questions.explanation: False. Gray matter includes cortex and subcortical nuclei and is associated with cell bodies, dendrites, and synapses.
choices: True
False
choiceExplanations: The word "only" makes this false: subcortical nuclei also contain gray matter. Gray matter is not restricted to the outer cerebral sheet.
Gray matter includes cerebral cortex and subcortical nuclei. Its presence below cortex is enough to reject the statement's absolute restriction.

questions.prompt: ERPs are derived by aligning and averaging EEG trials to an event.
questions.explanation: True. Averaging enhances event-locked activity relative to background activity that is not consistently time-locked. It does not make every source identifiable.
choices: True
False
choiceExplanations: Aligning EEG epochs to the same event and averaging corresponding time points emphasizes consistent event-locked activity relative to non-time-locked background.
Rejecting the statement would miss the defining ERP procedure. Averaging does not guarantee perfect source localization, but alignment and averaging are how ERPs are derived.

questions.prompt: fNIRS records the same magnetic-resonance BOLD signal as fMRI.
questions.explanation: False. fNIRS uses near-infrared light absorption to estimate changes in oxygenated/deoxygenated hemoglobin; both are indirect hemodynamic methods, but their measurement physics differ.
choices: True
False
choiceExplanations: Both methods concern hemodynamics, but their measurement physics differ. fNIRS uses light absorption rather than magnetic-resonance BOLD acquisition.

fNIRS estimates oxy/deoxyhemoglobin-related changes using near-infrared light; fMRI uses magnetic-resonance contrast related to blood oxygenation. Similar physiological targets do not make their signals identical.

questions.prompt: TMS reaches the hippocampus as directly and focally as a superficial cortical target.
questions.explanation: False. Conventional focal TMS primarily stimulates accessible superficial cortex; deep structures can be affected indirectly through networks, not targeted in the same way.
choices: True
False
choiceExplanations: Conventional focal TMS mainly reaches accessible superficial cortex. A deep structure such as the hippocampus is not targeted as directly and focally in the same way.
Deep structures can be influenced through connected networks, but indirect network effects differ from direct superficial targeting. That depth limitation makes the statement false.

questions.prompt: A double dissociation establishes that the two tasks never share any neural resources.
questions.explanation: False. Opposite selective impairments support differentiated resources, but tasks may also share resources and interact through networks.
choices: True
False
choiceExplanations: Opposite selective impairments support differentiated contributions. They do not establish zero shared resources, interactions, or overlapping processing stages.
The claim is too strong because partial specialization can coexist with shared resources. A double dissociation challenges a simple fixed difficulty ordering without proving complete independence.

questions.prompt: The yellow path illustrates a connection between the two cerebral hemispheres. Complete both blanks: The ______ is the major bundle connecting the hemispheres and is a ______ tract.
questions.explanation: Corpus callosum; commissural. It connects the hemispheres rather than merely two cortical sites within one hemisphere.
rubric: Corpus callosum
commissural. It connects the hemispheres rather than merely two cortical sites within one hemisphere.
commonMistakes: An association tract connects cortical sites within one hemisphere, so that label does not fit the corpus callosum's left-right connection. Projection describes cortical-subcortical/spinal endpoints rather than this commissural arrangement.

questions.prompt: Complete both blanks: The thalamus is a major sensory ______ to cortex; the classic initial-relay exception is ______.
questions.explanation: Relay; olfaction/smell. This exception does not mean the thalamus never participates in any olfactory processing.
rubric: Relay
olfaction/smell. This exception does not mean the thalamus never participates in any olfactory processing.
commonMistakes: The olfactory exception concerns an obligatory initial thalamic relay to primary olfactory cortex. Extending it to "smell never involves thalamus" incorrectly rules out later olfactory participation.

questions.prompt: Complete both blanks: Most neocortex is described as having ______ layers and an approximate thickness of ______ mm in this course.
questions.explanation: Six layers; about 3 mm. This is an approximate teaching value, not uniform thickness across every cortical region.
rubric: Six layers
about 3 mm. This is an approximate teaching value, not uniform thickness across every cortical region.
commonMistakes: Six layers describe microscopic organization through neocortical depth, not six surface folds. About 3 mm is a course approximation rather than a constant thickness at every point or a statement about every type of cortex.

questions.prompt: Complete both blanks: CNS myelin is formed by ______; resident immune/phagocytic glia are ______.
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes; microglia.
rubric: Oligodendrocytes
microglia.
commonMistakes: Microglia do not make CNS myelin; oligodendrocytes do. Microglia's immune/phagocytic role differs from myelination, and astrocytes' support roles do not make them interchangeable with either cell type.

questions.prompt: Complete both blanks: An individual action potential is approximately ______ in amplitude; a graded postsynaptic potential can ______ with other inputs.
questions.explanation: All-or-none / stereotyped; sum / combine spatially or temporally.
rubric: All-or-none / stereotyped
sum / combine spatially or temporally.
commonMistakes: Do not describe ordinary action potentials as graded simply because firing rate changes. Graded postsynaptic potentials can combine before threshold; action-potential amplitude is approximately stereotyped once triggered.

questions.prompt: A patient can initiate a reach but the trajectory is poorly coordinated and corrective movements are inaccurate. Name the relevant broad structure, give its role, and state two limits of inferring anatomy from this description.
questions.explanation: Cerebellum is the relevant broad candidate. It integrates planning/execution with sensory feedback to support smooth coordinated movement. Similar behavior can arise from other sensory/motor pathway problems. A behavioral vignette cannot uniquely localize a lesion without neurological/anatomical evidence.
rubric: Cerebellum is the relevant broad candidate.
It integrates planning/execution with sensory feedback to support smooth coordinated movement.
Similar behavior can arise from other sensory/motor pathway problems.
A behavioral vignette cannot uniquely localize a lesion without neurological/anatomical evidence.
commonMistakes: A coordination problem is not automatically a loss of muscle strength or definitive proof of one cerebellar lesion. Sensory feedback and other motor pathways can also affect trajectory, so the candidate needs anatomical and clinical testing.

questions.prompt: You need to know whether a rare target changes brain processing at about 300 ms. Select a method and paradigm, identify the signal, and explain one limitation.
questions.explanation: EEG/ERP with an oddball paradigm. Time-lock repeated trials to rare targets and examine a P300-family response. Signal is averaged event-related electrical population activity; the review places P300 roughly 250-500 ms after onset. Scalp localization is limited and a P300 is not a unique readout of a single mental state.
rubric: EEG/ERP with an oddball paradigm.
Time-lock repeated trials to rare targets and examine a P300-family response.
Signal is averaged event-related electrical population activity; the review places P300 roughly 250-500 ms after onset.
Scalp localization is limited and a P300 is not a unique readout of a single mental state.
commonMistakes: fMRI's slow hemodynamics are poorly suited to separating neural events around 300 ms. A P300-family response is not a unique thought detector and need not peak at precisely 300 ms or reveal one exact source.

questions.prompt: Distinguish local, sparse, and fully distributed coding. State which distinction a highly selective recorded neuron cannot resolve by itself.
questions.explanation: Strict local coding assigns a concept to one highly specific unit. Sparse coding uses a small subset of a population. Fully distributed coding represents concepts across much or all of a population's activity pattern. One selective recorded cell cannot distinguish strict one-cell-only storage from its participation in a sparse ensemble.
rubric: Strict local coding assigns a concept to one highly specific unit.
Sparse coding uses a small subset of a population.
Fully distributed coding represents concepts across much or all of a population's activity pattern.
One selective recorded cell cannot distinguish strict one-cell-only storage from its participation in a sparse ensemble.
commonMistakes: One highly selective cell does not tell you how many other cells carry the concept. Sparse coding can include very selective units, so selectivity alone cannot distinguish a sparse ensemble from a literal unique grandmother cell.

questions.prompt: Patient X is impaired on faces but spared on objects. Patient Y shows the opposite pattern. Identify the design logic, the alternative it challenges, and a remaining caution.
questions.explanation: This is a double dissociation. Opposite selective impairments suggest partially distinct resources. It challenges a simple single-resource account in which one task is always harder. Performance baselines, perceptual demands, lesion variation, and network effects still require controls.
rubric: This is a double dissociation.
Opposite selective impairments suggest partially distinct resources.
It challenges a simple single-resource account in which one task is always harder.
Performance baselines, perceptual demands, lesion variation, and network effects still require controls.
commonMistakes: Do not collapse the two opposite impairments into a single dissociation or claim that they prove zero shared resources. The reversal challenges a simple fixed task-difficulty ordering while still allowing interaction and overlap.

questions.prompt: Choose one method to measure involvement and one to test causal contribution in a cortical task. Explain why the conclusions differ.
questions.explanation: fMRI can measure a task-related BOLD contrast indicating involvement. TMS can perturb an accessible cortical site while behavior is measured. Measurement alone is correlational; controlled perturbation changes the system. Selective behavioral disruption supports a causal contribution/conditional necessity, with control-site, sham, timing, and nonspecific effects considered.
rubric: fMRI can measure a task-related BOLD contrast indicating involvement.
TMS can perturb an accessible cortical site while behavior is measured.
Measurement alone is correlational; controlled perturbation changes the system.
Selective behavioral disruption supports a causal contribution/conditional necessity, with control-site, sham, timing, and nonspecific effects considered.
commonMistakes: Observing greater activity during a task does not show that the task requires the region. Perturbation is a different evidential step, and its behavioral effects still need controls for nonspecific stimulation effects.

questions.prompt: Describe the CNS/PNS division and distinguish cerebrum from cerebellum. Explain why cortex, cerebrum, and brain are not interchangeable terms.
questions.explanation: CNS is brain plus spinal cord; PNS is outside CNS. Cerebrum includes the cerebral hemispheres with cortex and deeper structures. Cerebellum is a distinct posterior/inferior brain structure. Cerebral cortex is the outer cerebral gray-matter sheet, not the entire cerebrum or entire brain.
rubric: CNS is brain plus spinal cord; PNS is outside CNS.
Cerebrum includes the cerebral hemispheres with cortex and deeper structures.
Cerebellum is a distinct posterior/inferior brain structure.
Cerebral cortex is the outer cerebral gray-matter sheet, not the entire cerebrum or entire brain.
commonMistakes: The cerebellum is part of the brain but is not the cerebrum. The cerebral cortex is only the outer cerebral sheet; substituting "cortex" for the whole brain leaves out deeper and noncerebral structures.

questions.prompt: On the lateral schematic, identify regions 1-4 and one broad function of each. Use front/back and the sulci rather than memorized illustration colors.
questions.explanation: 1 frontal: voluntary motor/executive functions. 2 parietal: somatosensory/spatial processing. 3 temporal: hearing/recognition and related functions. 4 occipital: visual processing. This gross-anatomy drill supplements the guide's cortex category; left of image is anterior.
rubric: 1 frontal: voluntary motor/executive functions.
2 parietal: somatosensory/spatial processing.
3 temporal: hearing/recognition and related functions.
4 occipital: visual processing. This gross-anatomy drill supplements the guide's cortex category; left of image is anterior.
commonMistakes: Lobe colors are arbitrary and can change between illustrations. Orient anterior/posterior and use sulci and adjacency; broad lobe functions are useful labels rather than exclusive storage locations for whole behaviors.

questions.prompt: Define dorsal, ventral, rostral, caudal, medial, and lateral for the forebrain. Give two correct anatomical relationships.
questions.explanation: Dorsal is superior/top; ventral is inferior/bottom. Rostral is anterior/front; caudal is posterior/back. Medial is toward midline; lateral is away from it. Two accurate examples, such as hypothalamus ventral to thalamus and frontal cortex rostral to occipital cortex. Specify orientation because the neuraxis bends.
rubric: Dorsal is superior/top; ventral is inferior/bottom.
Rostral is anterior/front; caudal is posterior/back.
Medial is toward midline; lateral is away from it.
Two accurate examples, such as hypothalamus ventral to thalamus and frontal cortex rostral to occipital cortex. Specify orientation because the neuraxis bends.
commonMistakes: Medial does not mean left and lateral does not mean right. Both sides of the brain have medial and lateral locations, and directional conventions must specify the relevant part of the bent neuraxis.

questions.prompt: Explain gyri, sulci, cortical folding, and why the two banks of the central sulcus matter functionally.
questions.explanation: Gyri are ridges; sulci are grooves. Folding accommodates more cortical surface within head size. Primary motor cortex is just anterior to central sulcus. Primary somatosensory cortex is just posterior; the boundary helps orient functional anatomy but complex functions extend beyond one ridge.
rubric: Gyri are ridges; sulci are grooves.
Folding accommodates more cortical surface within head size.
Primary motor cortex is just anterior to central sulcus.
Primary somatosensory cortex is just posterior; the boundary helps orient functional anatomy but complex functions extend beyond one ridge.
commonMistakes: Gyri are ridges and sulci are grooves, not the reverse. Primary motor and somatosensory cortex lie on opposite sides of the central sulcus, so confusing its banks reverses this functional landmark.

questions.prompt: Distinguish layers from columns in neocortex. State approximate thickness and layer count, and explain why folding is not another word for either.
questions.explanation: Neocortex is about 3 mm thick in the introductory description and has six layers. Layers reflect cellular organization across cortical depth. Columns/minicolumns are vertically organized circuits spanning layers. Gyri/sulci are larger-scale folds of the sheet, not the microscopic layering or column structure.
rubric: Neocortex is about 3 mm thick in the introductory description and has six layers.
Layers reflect cellular organization across cortical depth.
Columns/minicolumns are vertically organized circuits spanning layers.
Gyri/sulci are larger-scale folds of the sheet, not the microscopic layering or column structure.
commonMistakes: Layers, columns, and folds occur at different scales. Layers run through cortical depth, columns span layers, and gyri/sulci fold the entire sheet; none is just another name for the others.

questions.prompt: Describe all four ways to categorize cortical areas and give an example of what evidence each uses.
questions.explanation: Surface anatomy: gyri/sulci and visible landmarks. Cytoarchitecture: microscopic cell/layer organization, as in Brodmann's scheme. Function: response or behavioral role, as in primary visual cortex. Connectivity: patterns of inputs/outputs to other areas. The schemes need not yield identical boundaries.
rubric: Surface anatomy: gyri/sulci and visible landmarks.
Cytoarchitecture: microscopic cell/layer organization, as in Brodmann's scheme.
Function: response or behavioral role, as in primary visual cortex.
Connectivity: patterns of inputs/outputs to other areas. The schemes need not yield identical boundaries.
commonMistakes: Brodmann classification is based on cytoarchitecture, not directly on a complete behavioral test. Surface landmarks, cell organization, response/function, and connectivity provide different evidence and need not produce identical boundaries.

questions.prompt: A region's cells resemble one area microscopically but it connects to several other systems. Explain why cytoarchitecture alone may not fully specify function and why connectivity matters.
questions.explanation: Cytoarchitecture describes cellular arrangement rather than a complete computation. Inputs determine available information. Outputs determine which other systems can use/transmit its results. Functional evidence and connectivity complement microstructure; no one classification alone exhausts what an area does.
rubric: Cytoarchitecture describes cellular arrangement rather than a complete computation.
Inputs determine available information.
Outputs determine which other systems can use/transmit its results.
Functional evidence and connectivity complement microstructure; no one classification alone exhausts what an area does.
commonMistakes: A similar-looking cellular arrangement does not specify every input, output, or computation. Connectivity matters because it constrains the information an area receives and which other systems can use its processing.

questions.prompt: Compare cortical gray matter, subcortical gray matter, white matter, and ventricles by composition and location.
questions.explanation: Cortex is an outer sheet enriched in neuronal cell bodies/dendrites/synapses. Subcortical nuclei are gray-matter clusters below cortex. White matter contains axons, often myelinated, and supporting glia; it is not a collection of whole neurons only. Ventricles are internal CSF-filled spaces, not another neural tissue type.
rubric: Cortex is an outer sheet enriched in neuronal cell bodies/dendrites/synapses.
Subcortical nuclei are gray-matter clusters below cortex.
White matter contains axons, often myelinated, and supporting glia; it is not a collection of whole neurons only.
Ventricles are internal CSF-filled spaces, not another neural tissue type.
commonMistakes: Gray matter is not restricted to cortex, and white matter is not just a pile of complete neuronal cell bodies. Subcortical nuclei are gray matter; ventricles are fluid-filled spaces rather than another neural tissue category.

questions.prompt: Use the yellow cortex-to-lower-CNS path as one example. Describe association, commissural, and projection pathways by their cortex/hemisphere/subcortex endpoints. Give one example of each and explain why 'projection' does not mean 'crosses hemispheres.'
questions.explanation: Association: cortex to cortex within a hemisphere; SLF is an example. Commissural: between hemispheres; corpus callosum is an example. Projection: cortex with subcortical/spinal levels; corticospinal tract is an example. The class depends on which levels/regions it connects; projection pathways can have crossings, but crossing hemispheres is not their defining property.
rubric: Association: cortex to cortex within a hemisphere; SLF is an example.
Commissural: between hemispheres; corpus callosum is an example.
Projection: cortex with subcortical/spinal levels; corticospinal tract is an example.
The class depends on which levels/regions it connects; projection pathways can have crossings, but crossing hemispheres is not their defining property.
commonMistakes: Classify pathways by their endpoints, not by the word "projection" or by any crossing alone. Association is within-hemisphere cortex-to-cortex; commissural links hemispheres; projection links cortex with subcortical/spinal levels.

questions.prompt: The yellow path illustrates a cortex-to-lower-CNS connection. Classify four hypothetical bundles: left temporal to left frontal cortex; left cortex to right cortex; cortex to spinal cord; neighboring cortical gyri within one hemisphere. Justify each.
questions.explanation: Left temporal-frontal: association. Left-right cortical connection: commissural. Cortex-spinal connection: projection. Neighboring same-hemisphere cortical gyri: short association/U-fibers. Endpoint relationships, not length alone, determine the main class.
rubric: Left temporal-frontal: association.
Left-right cortical connection: commissural.
Cortex-spinal connection: projection.
Neighboring same-hemisphere cortical gyri: short association/U-fibers. Endpoint relationships, not length alone, determine the main class.
commonMistakes: A very short connection between neighboring gyri is still an association pathway. Length alone does not make a tract a projection tract; cortex-to-spinal endpoints do.

questions.prompt: Explain how white-matter damage could impair a task despite preserved cell bodies in the two cortical regions normally supporting it. Contrast this with direct cortical damage.
questions.explanation: Axons transmit information between regions. Damaged tracts can disrupt communication/timing despite locally viable gray matter. Direct cortical damage can disrupt processing at a node itself. The same behavioral deficit can therefore reflect node or connection damage; a simple location-to-function inference can miss network disconnection.
rubric: Axons transmit information between regions.
Damaged tracts can disrupt communication/timing despite locally viable gray matter.
Direct cortical damage can disrupt processing at a node itself.
The same behavioral deficit can therefore reflect node or connection damage; a simple location-to-function inference can miss network disconnection.
commonMistakes: Preserved cell bodies do not guarantee an intact functioning network. Damaged connecting axons can prevent regions from exchanging information even when local gray matter remains viable.

questions.prompt: Define ventricles and CSF. Explain mechanical protection, chemical/homeostatic roles, and why CSF should not be described as a white-matter tract.
questions.explanation: Ventricles are cavities containing cerebrospinal fluid. CSF cushions/supports the brain mechanically. CSF contributes to stable conditions, waste clearance, and pressure regulation. A fluid-filled space is not an axon bundle or a neuron cluster.
rubric: Ventricles are cavities containing cerebrospinal fluid.
CSF cushions/supports the brain mechanically.
CSF contributes to stable conditions, waste clearance, and pressure regulation.
A fluid-filled space is not an axon bundle or a neuron cluster.
commonMistakes: CSF is a fluid and ventricles are spaces containing it; neither is an association tract or a gray-matter nucleus. Mechanical protection and homeostatic roles do not make CSF a substitute for neuronal signaling.

questions.prompt: Describe the basal ganglia at the level shown in the review. Include broad location, the three named component structures, action regulation, learning, and a distinction from cerebellar coordination.
questions.explanation: The basal ganglia are a group of deep structures present in both cerebral hemispheres. The review names caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus. These are the listed examples, not a claim that the broader basal-ganglia system has no other components. They contribute to regulating, selecting/planning, and terminating actions, and to reward, skill, and habit learning. The cerebellum emphasizes coordination and sensory-feedback integration. Both contribute to movement, but their broad roles differ.
rubric: The basal ganglia are a group of deep structures present in both cerebral hemispheres.
The review names caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus. These are the listed examples, not a claim that the broader basal-ganglia system has no other components.
They contribute to regulating, selecting/planning, and terminating actions, and to reward, skill, and habit learning.
The cerebellum emphasizes coordination and sensory-feedback integration. Both contribute to movement, but their broad roles differ.
commonMistakes: Do not describe basal ganglia as a single white-matter cable or claim the three course-listed structures exhaust every broader definition. Action regulation and habit/reward learning also differ from the cerebellar emphasis on coordination and feedback.

questions.prompt: Contrast hippocampus and amygdala by broad location and role and use a patient scenario to distinguish them. Give one limit of the labels 'memory center' and 'fear center.'
questions.explanation: Hippocampus lies in medial temporal regions, posterior to amygdala, and is important for new learning/memory formation. Amygdala lies in anterior medial temporal regions and contributes to threat and other emotional processing. A new-memory deficit versus altered emotional/threat response motivates different candidate systems. Neither label captures all functions or isolates all memory/emotion in one site; interaction and other structures matter.
rubric: Hippocampus lies in medial temporal regions, posterior to amygdala, and is important for new learning/memory formation.
Amygdala lies in anterior medial temporal regions and contributes to threat and other emotional processing.
A new-memory deficit versus altered emotional/threat response motivates different candidate systems.
Neither label captures all functions or isolates all memory/emotion in one site; interaction and other structures matter.
commonMistakes: "Memory center" and "fear center" are incomplete labels. Memory and emotion involve interacting systems, and the hippocampus and amygdala are medial temporal structures with different broad contributions rather than one interchangeable site.

questions.prompt: Distinguish thalamus and hypothalamus in location and sensory/endocrine role. Name the larger brain division containing both, and give two specific examples of hypothalamic regulation.
questions.explanation: Thalamus is a deep, near-midline relay between many sensory systems and cortex, organized into nuclei. Hypothalamus lies below the thalamus and links neural and endocrine regulation. Both belong to the diencephalon. Temperature regulation is one hypothalamic example. Hunger, thirst, sexual activity, or caregiving regulation provides a second example. Their similar names do not imply the same function.
rubric: Thalamus is a deep, near-midline relay between many sensory systems and cortex, organized into nuclei.
Hypothalamus lies below the thalamus and links neural and endocrine regulation. Both belong to the diencephalon.
Temperature regulation is one hypothalamic example.
Hunger, thirst, sexual activity, or caregiving regulation provides a second example. Their similar names do not imply the same function.
commonMistakes: The similar names do not imply the same function. Thalamus is the major sensory-relay comparison; hypothalamus lies below it and links bodily regulation with endocrine control. Both are in the diencephalon, not different names for the cerebellum.

questions.prompt: Explain the olfactory exception to the classic thalamic sensory-relay rule. State why 'smell never involves the thalamus' is too strong, and distinguish olfactory bulbs from the thalamus.
questions.explanation: Initial olfactory input can reach primary olfactory cortex without the obligatory first thalamic relay of many other senses. This does not exclude later thalamic participation in olfactory processing. Olfactory bulbs are early smell-processing structures. Their sensory input contributes to detection and connections with mood/memory; thalamus has a broader relay role.
rubric: Initial olfactory input can reach primary olfactory cortex without the obligatory first thalamic relay of many other senses.
This does not exclude later thalamic participation in olfactory processing.
Olfactory bulbs are early smell-processing structures.
Their sensory input contributes to detection and connections with mood/memory; thalamus has a broader relay role.
commonMistakes: Bypassing an obligatory initial thalamic relay does not mean smell has no later thalamic processing. Olfactory bulbs are early olfactory structures, not renamed thalamic nuclei.

questions.prompt: What functions are associated with the cingulate gyrus and olfactory bulbs in the review? Explain how these extend the core guide's emphasis on hippocampus and amygdala.
questions.explanation: Cingulate gyrus is associated with emotional/cognitive conflict. Olfactory bulbs process smell-related input. Smell can be important for stimulus detection, mood, and memory. These are additional limbic-related labels in the review; the one-page guide emphasizes hippocampus/amygdala, and the cingulate gyrus is cortical rather than literally a subcortical nucleus.
rubric: Cingulate gyrus is associated with emotional/cognitive conflict.
Olfactory bulbs process smell-related input.
Smell can be important for stimulus detection, mood, and memory.
These are additional limbic-related labels in the review; the one-page guide emphasizes hippocampus/amygdala, and the cingulate gyrus is cortical rather than literally a subcortical nucleus.
commonMistakes: Calling every limbic-related structure a subcortical nucleus misclassifies the cingulate gyrus, which is cortex. Olfactory bulbs concern smell processing, not the same conflict-related role assigned to cingulate cortex in the review.

questions.prompt: Explain cerebellar contributions to posture, dexterity, smooth movement, and integration of action planning/execution with feedback. State why preserved muscle strength would not rule out a cerebellar problem.
questions.explanation: It supports posture/balance-related control. It contributes to dexterous, well-timed movement. Comparing/integrating action plans and sensory feedback supports smooth corrections. Coordination can fail despite adequate force; strength and movement organization are different aspects of performance.
rubric: It supports posture/balance-related control.
It contributes to dexterous, well-timed movement.
Comparing/integrating action plans and sensory feedback supports smooth corrections.
Coordination can fail despite adequate force; strength and movement organization are different aspects of performance.
commonMistakes: Adequate force does not guarantee well-timed, accurate movement. A person can have strength while impaired feedback integration and coordination disrupt posture, trajectory, and corrective movements.

questions.prompt: Describe a typical neuron and identify input, integration, conduction, and output structures. Explain why the review's cell counts do not mean most CNS neurons are in cerebral cortex.
questions.explanation: Dendrites/soma commonly receive inputs; the soma supports the cell. Integration near hillock/initial segment can initiate an AP. Axon conducts and terminals provide synaptic output. The review gives about 86 billion brain neurons and about 19% of CNS neurons in cerebral cortex; a large cortical volume does not imply a majority of neuron count.
rubric: Dendrites/soma commonly receive inputs; the soma supports the cell.
Integration near hillock/initial segment can initiate an AP.
Axon conducts and terminals provide synaptic output.
The review gives about 86 billion brain neurons and about 19% of CNS neurons in cerebral cortex; a large cortical volume does not imply a majority of neuron count.
commonMistakes: A large cortical volume is not the same as a majority of neurons. Keep the approximate brain count and the review's cortical proportion separate, and preserve the neuron's input-integration-axon-output sequence.

questions.prompt: Compare action potentials and postsynaptic potentials in size, propagation, summation, and their roles in communication.
questions.explanation: APs are stereotyped all-or-none events; postsynaptic potentials are graded. APs regenerate along axons; passive graded changes attenuate with distance. Postsynaptic inputs sum across time/locations to influence threshold. AP rate can influence transmitter release and the postsynaptic response, but one incoming AP does not guarantee an outgoing AP.
rubric: APs are stereotyped all-or-none events; postsynaptic potentials are graded.
APs regenerate along axons; passive graded changes attenuate with distance.
Postsynaptic inputs sum across time/locations to influence threshold.
AP rate can influence transmitter release and the postsynaptic response, but one incoming AP does not guarantee an outgoing AP.
commonMistakes: Postsynaptic inputs can sum without necessarily producing a spike. Do not add spike heights to explain intensity or assume that every presynaptic spike makes the next neuron fire.

questions.prompt: Sequence transmission through a chemical synapse and explain what 'electrochemical' means. Include the role of the axon hillock/initial segment.
questions.explanation: Electrical inputs combine near the trigger region; threshold initiates a regenerating AP. The AP reaches the terminal and triggers transmitter release. Chemical transmitter crosses the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors. Receptor effects change ionic conductances/postsynaptic electrical signals, which contribute to the next firing decision.
rubric: Electrical inputs combine near the trigger region; threshold initiates a regenerating AP.
The AP reaches the terminal and triggers transmitter release.
Chemical transmitter crosses the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors.
Receptor effects change ionic conductances/postsynaptic electrical signals, which contribute to the next firing decision.
commonMistakes: In a chemical synapse the same electrical impulse does not cross an empty gap into the next cell. The sequence changes from electrical conduction to chemical receptor signaling and back to a postsynaptic electrical influence.

questions.prompt: Assign the correct glial type to CNS myelination, immune phagocytosis, and synaptic/BBB support. Repair the claim that astrocytes alone form the physical blood-brain barrier.
questions.explanation: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons. Microglia provide resident immune/phagocytic functions. Astrocytes support synaptic function and BBB regulation/maintenance. Endothelial tight junctions form the principal physical barrier; astrocytes are important supporting participants, not the entire barrier by themselves.
rubric: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons.
Microglia provide resident immune/phagocytic functions.
Astrocytes support synaptic function and BBB regulation/maintenance.
Endothelial tight junctions form the principal physical barrier; astrocytes are important supporting participants, not the entire barrier by themselves.
commonMistakes: Astrocytes help regulate and maintain the BBB but do not alone make its principal physical seal; endothelial tight junctions do. Distinguish that support role from oligodendrocyte myelination and microglial immune functions.

questions.prompt: Explain how myelin damage can impair communication without making each surviving action potential 'half as tall.' Distinguish conduction from coding of stimulus strength.
questions.explanation: Myelin promotes rapid efficient conduction between excitable axonal segments. Demyelination can slow or block reliable conduction. AP amplitude remains stereotyped where an AP is successfully regenerated; failure/latency is not simply a smaller encoded spike. Rate/population patterns can encode intensity; conduction reliability is a different issue.
rubric: Myelin promotes rapid efficient conduction between excitable axonal segments.
Demyelination can slow or block reliable conduction.
AP amplitude remains stereotyped where an AP is successfully regenerated; failure/latency is not simply a smaller encoded spike.
Rate/population patterns can encode intensity; conduction reliability is a different issue.
commonMistakes: Demyelination concerns the speed and reliability of conduction, including possible block. It is not a simple analog volume control that makes every successfully regenerated action potential half-sized.

questions.prompt: Compare single-unit recording, EEG/ERP, structural MRI, fMRI, fNIRS, organic lesions, and TMS. For each state the signal/intervention, invasiveness or acquisition context, one strength, and one limitation.
questions.explanation: Single-unit: extracellular spikes; invasive electrode access; millisecond timing and individual-neuron sampling; sparse, region-limited samples and limited generalizability from clinical populations. EEG/ERP: scalp voltages/event-locked averages, largely reflecting population postsynaptic activity; noninvasive; excellent timing and relatively low cost; poor source localization and electrical/movement artifacts. Structural MRI: tissue/water magnetic-resonance properties; noninvasive; detailed anatomical localization; a structural snapshot does not directly measure neural task activity, and stillness/scanner tolerance matter. fMRI: BOLD contrast from blood oxygenation; noninvasive; fine spatial localization and whole-brain task comparisons; indirect, slow hemodynamics and motion sensitivity. fNIRS: near-infrared absorption changes related to oxy/deoxyhemoglobin; noninvasive scalp optodes; portability and relatively greater movement tolerance; superficial coverage, low spatial resolution, and slow hemodynamic timing. Organic lesions: acquired damage rather than a researcher-assigned invasive procedure; can reveal causal dependence of behavior on affected systems; lesion variability, unknown premorbid ability, secondary effects, and reorganization complicate inference. TMS: induced currents perturb cortical firing; nonsurgical/noninvasive stimulation; permits site/time and within-person causal tests; mainly superficial targeting, broad network effects, sound/sensation, and need for suitable controls.
rubric: Single-unit: extracellular spikes; invasive electrode access; millisecond timing and individual-neuron sampling; sparse, region-limited samples and limited generalizability from clinical populations.
